label: priestly blessing and tithing
why: Exodus 28 and Leviticus 1-2 emphasize Aaron's role in presenting offerings, using the root קָרַב and naming Aaron explicitly.

label: Covenant and deliverance
why: Exodus 6:1-8 and Exodus 15:1-13 emphasize God's covenant with Israel and His redemptive deliverance from Egypt, using forms of בְּרִית (covenant) and גָּאַל (to redeem).

label: Prohibition of idolatry and sorcery
why: Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 use these terms to prohibit idolatrous and immoral practices, including sorcery and incest.

label: Justice and Fairness
why: Leviticus 25 and Exodus 23 emphasize the duty to act justly and redeem or protect one’s compatriot, especially the poor or vulnerable.

label: Enoch's unique fate
why: Genesis 5:21-24 describes Enoch being taken by God without dying, making this phrase unique to his fate.

label: Lineage and Human Development
why: The passages repeatedly use 'יָלַד' (to beget) and 'חָיָה' (to live) to trace lineage and human development through generations.

label: Covenantal promise and people's response
why: Exodus 19:4-8, Leviticus 9:1, and Deuteronomy 5:1-3 emphasize the covenant (בְּרִית) and the people's collective response as an assembly (עֵדָה).

label: Festivals and Worship
why: These offerings are central to the festivals and worship described in Numbers 28-29 and other passages, representing both devotion and communal celebration.

label: Consequences and shame
why: Genesis 3:8-13 and Leviticus 4-5 use these terms to describe the consequences of sin and the resulting shame and need for atonement.

label: Negotiation and labor terms
why: Genesis 30:25-34, 37-42 uses these terms to describe Jacob's negotiation of his wages through the management of flocks and troughs.

label: Theft and Restitution
why: The passages emphasize טָמֵא (unclean) in relation to bodily discharges, contact with carcasses, and leprous conditions, and כִּפּוּר (atonement) in the context of purification and restitution.

label: Divine Character
why: Passages like Leviticus 19:2 and Leviticus 20:7-8 emphasize the centrality of holiness in divine character, with קָדוֹשׁ (holy) and יְהֹוָה (LORD) recurring as foundational to God's nature and the ethical demands He makes.

label: Construction of the Tabernacle
why: Exodus 26:33, 27:21, 38:8, and 40:2, 40:28 use this exact phrase to refer to the central structure where God meets with Israel.

label: Generational lineage
why: The phrase 'יָלַד' (to beget) and the repeated genealogical structures in passages like Genesis 5 and 10 emphasize the theme of generational lineage through the naming and birth of sons.

label: Hope through Noah
why: Exodus 2:23-25 and Leviticus 26:44-45 emphasize God's covenant and its restoration, while Genesis 5:28-30 hints at life through Noah.

label: God's covenant with humanity and creation
why: Passages like Genesis 9:8-17 and Exodus 29:42-46 use בְּרִית (covenant) and emphasize life (חַיִּים) in God's promises to humanity and creation.

label: God's promise to Abram
why: Genesis 17:7-8 and Genesis 17:19-21 emphasize God's covenant with Abraham, promising an everlasting posterity (zera le'olam) as the core of the promise.

label: Warning Against Idolatry
gloss: you shall not make an idol
why: Exodus 34:14-17 and Deuteronomy 5:8-9 (implied in the theme) use forms of לֹא (not), פֶּסֶל (idol), and the prohibition against making or worshiping idols as central to the warning against idolatry.

label: Creation of the world
why: Genesis 1:1-31 repeatedly uses this phrase to describe the act of creation.

label: Preparation of the earth
why: Genesis 2:5-6 describes the earth as desolate before human cultivation, and the theme continues through the preparation and division of the earth in service, war, and covenant.

label: God's judgment
why: The passages emphasize God's action to set apart, isolate, or distinguish (as in separating nations, defiling practices, or keeping the covenant), often through judgment.

label: Dinah's violation
why: The passages center on the family journey from Canaan to Egypt, Joseph's role in Egypt, and Jacob's response, making their names central to the theme.

label: Sabbatical and Rest
why: Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15 put it this way, connecting the sabbatical year with the jubilee and the release of debts and servants.

label: Balaam's attempts to curse Israel
why: The passages repeatedly describe Balaam's attempts (קָבַב) to curse Israel at Balak's request, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Human creation and dominion
gloss: created in our image and given dominion
why: Genesis 1:26-28 puts it this way, stating that humans are created in the image of God and given dominion over the earth and its creatures.

label: Creation of the human
why: Genesis 2:7 describes the human being formed from dust (earth) and given life, making this phrase central to the theme of creation of the human.

label: Garden of Eden
why: Genesis 2:8-14, 15 uses this exact phrase to describe the paradise where the human is placed.

label: Longevity and mortality
why: Genesis 5:3-31 repeatedly uses forms of חָיָה ('live') and records deaths, emphasizing the theme of longevity and mortality.

label: Settlement and land
why: The passages repeatedly use terms like גְּבוּל (border) and reference the land (אָרֶץ), especially in Numbers 34 and Deuteronomy 3, which detail the boundaries and division of the land.

label: Instructions to the Israelites
why: Leviticus 9:2-18 and Numbers 6:14-21 use this phrase to describe the Israelites' ritual actions, including burnt, sin, and peace offerings.

label: Genealogies and lineage
why: Exodus 6:14-25 and Numbers 26:5-50, 57-62 use these terms to describe the detailed listings of family lines and ancestry.

label: Fear of God
why: The phrase 'יִרְאַת יְהוָה' (fear of the Lord) is central to passages like Deuteronomy 10:12-13 and Deuteronomy 8:6, where reverence for God is tied to obedience, love, and keeping His commandments.

label: Protection of the vulnerable
why: Exodus 22:20-23, Deuteronomy 10:14-19, and Deuteronomy 24:6, 17 put it this way, emphasizing the protection of these vulnerable groups.

label: Idolatry and the golden calf
why: Exodus 32:1-6, 21-25 directly describe the Israelites making and worshiping a golden calf, which becomes the central symbol of idolatry in these passages.

label: Ritual purity and uncleanness
why: Leviticus 15 and Numbers 5-4 emphasize the distinction and processes of becoming tamei (unclean) or tahor (clean).

label: Replacement of Abel
why: Genesis 4:25-26 and 5:1-2 present Seth as the generational replacement for Abel, and 'תּוֹלֵדוֹת' (generations) is a key term in the narrative of lineage continuation.

label: Divine judgment on humanity
why: Passages like Genesis 19 and Deuteronomy 9 emphasize divine destruction of the wicked, using words like שָׁחַת and רִשְׁעָה.

label: Divine Call and Promise
why: The passages emphasize God's leading (דֶּ֫רֶךְ) and divine action (אֵל) in calling and promising to His people.

label: Divine vision and promise
why: The passages emphasize divine promises and blessings from a father (Jacob) to his sons, especially in Genesis 48 and 49, where the language of blessing (בְּרָכָה) and fatherhood (אָב) is central.

label: Death and Burial
why: These two verbs appear together in the passages describing the death and burial of key figures like Rachel, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph.

label: Consecration and redemption of firstborns
why: Exodus 13 and Leviticus 12-14 use these terms to describe the consecration of firstborns and the associated purification rituals.

label: Human disobedience
why: This phrase captures the tension and conflict in passages like Genesis 16 and Deuteronomy 1, where human disobedience leads to strife, especially in relation to life, conception, and divine will.

label: Exile and protection
why: Passages like Genesis 19 (fleeing Sodom) and Genesis 8 (the ark) use forms of צוּק (to press/siege) and תֵּבָה (ark), central to the theme of exile and protection.

label: Cain's Sin and Consequences
why: This phrase captures the central motif of selling or losing one's rightful possession, as seen in Cain's loss of divine favor, Esau's sale of his birthright, and the Israelites' loss of the land due to disobedience.

label: Barrenness and family
why: The passages focus on the inability to conceive (הָרָה) and the resulting concerns about inheritance (נַחֲלָה), especially in the stories of Sarai, Hagar, and Zelophehad's daughters.

label: Abram's Obedience and Journey
why: The passages emphasize Abram's journey and obedience, particularly in Genesis 12:4-8 and 13:18, where his movement and faith are central.

label: Moral Dilemma and Consequences
why: This phrase captures the recurring moral dilemmas involving familial relationships (sister/wife) and tribal inheritance (matteh), as seen in the stories of Abram, Abraham, Isaac, and Zelophehad’s daughters.

label: Purification and Worship
why: The passages emphasize the altar (מִזְבֵּחַ) and the act of offering (קָטַר), central to the rituals of purification and worship.

label: Family division and conflict
why: Genesis 42:21-22 and Genesis 37 highlight conflict and division between brothers, especially among Joseph and his siblings.

label: Joseph's Continued Influence
why: The passages emphasize Joseph's presence, influence, and role in Egypt, from imprisonment to leadership, and his management of food during famine.

label: Complaints and leadership challenges
why: The passages in Exodus and Numbers repeatedly use 'לוּן' (to grumble) and 'בֵּן עֶשְׂרִים' (son of twenty) to describe the complaints and leadership challenges of the Israelite generation.

label: Hardening of Pharaoh's heart
why: Exodus 7:3, 10:1, 11:10, and other passages repeatedly use this phrase to describe Pharaoh's unyielding resistance.

label: Passover instructions
why: Exodus 12:1-23, 24-42, 43-51, and Exodus 13:3-9, 14-16 use 'פֶּ֫סַח' (Passover) as the central term for the ritual and its observance.

label: Voluntary Offerings
why: Exodus 35:20-29 and Numbers 7:10-88 describe the voluntary offerings brought by the Israelites, using terms like קָרְבַּן (offering) and emphasizing the act of giving.

label: Construction of the Ark
why: Exodus 37:1-9 describes the construction of the ark and its mercy seat, and 'mispachat' is used in the context of the ark's construction.

label: God's approval
why: Genesis 1:31 uses this exact phrase to describe God's evaluation of His creation, encapsulating His approval.

label: Creation of the woman
gloss: a side from which to make
why: Genesis 2:21-22 describes the making of the woman from the man's side, forming a union.

label: The serpent's temptation
why: Genesis 3:1-5 directly references the serpent (נָחָשׁ) and the fruit (פְּרִי) of the tree (עֵץ) as central to the temptation.

label: God's regret and sorrow
why: Genesis 6:6-7 and Genesis 18:23-32 show God expressing sorrow and reconsidering His judgment, using the word נָחַם (to be sorry, relent) in both contexts.

label: Eber and the division of the earth
why: Genesis 10:25 notes the birth of Peleg, whose name signifies the division of the earth during his time.

label: Divine Encounter and Covenant
why: Exodus 3 and Genesis 12-15 center on divine encounters with Moses and Abram, both involving God's covenantal promises and the context of Egypt.

label: Lot's choice and separation
gloss: to take for himself to water
why: Genesis 13:10-11 and Numbers 32:1-5 highlight choices involving land and water, with 'שָׁקָה' (to water) and 'לָקַח' (to take) central to the theme of separation and possession.

label: Family conflict and resentment
why: The passages emphasize vows (נֶ֫דֶר) and rash words (מִבְטָא) as central to the tensions and conflicts within family dynamics, especially in Numbers 30 and Genesis 27.

label: Divine guidance through cloud and fire
why: Exodus 13:21-22 and Numbers 9:15-23 describe the cloud and fire as the visible signs of God's guidance.

label: Water Crisis and Testing God
why: Deuteronomy 33:2-29 uses 'machaneh' (camp) and 'yeshurun' (Jeshurun) to describe the organized and protected people of God, reflecting both the crisis and divine provision in their journey.

label: Divine commandments
why: Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 refer to the commandments as divine words (דָּבָר), and the plural form דְּבָרִים is used in Deuteronomy 17 to refer to the law and commandments collectively.

label: Caring for Others
why: Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 15 emphasize not closing one's heart to the poor and afflicted, using related language and themes.

label: Conquest and Divine Guidance
why: These passages emphasize the divine command to drive out (גָּרַשׁ) and destroy (חָרַם) the nations and their idolatry in Canaan.

label: Divine anger and judgment
why: Exodus 32:7-10 and Leviticus 10:1-2 depict God's anger (אַף) in response to sin and idolatry, central to the theme of divine judgment.

label: Building the Table for Showbread
why: Exodus 37:10-16 describes the making and arrangement of the table for showbread, using both 'עָרַךְ' (to arrange) and 'שֻׁלְחָן' (table).

label: Preparation of Sacred Items
why: The passages emphasize the Levites' role in preparing and maintaining sacred items and their inheritance of cities and duties within the congregation.

label: The flood as a divine solution
why: Genesis 6-7 describe the flood (מַבּוּל) and the ark (תֵּבָה) as central to God's action and salvation.

label: Noah's righteousness and favor
why: Genesis 6:8-9 describes Noah as righteous and finding חֶסֶד (favor) in God's eyes, which is central to the theme.

label: Instructions for entering the ark
why: This phrase captures the central idea of listing or accounting for every living being, as seen in the command to bring every living creature into the ark (Gen 7:2-9) and the census with a half-shekel contribution for every soul (Exod 30:12-

label: Conflict between Abram and Lot
why: Genesis 14:1-11 describes a war between four kings and five kings, framing the conflict in which Abram and Lot are involved.

label: Vows and sacred naming
why: Jacob makes a vow (נֶ֫דֶר) and names (שֵׁם) the place Bethel, and the theme of sacred naming and vows recurs in Leviticus with valuation (עֵ֫רֶךְ) and setting (שׂוּם) of sacred commitments.

label: Family rivalry and competition
why: Genesis 30:1-15, 16-21 put it this way through the rivalry between Leah, Rachel, and their maidservants over Jacob.

label: Reconciliation and reunion
why: This phrase captures the emotional and reconciliatory tone of the passages, especially in Genesis 33 and 45, where reconciliation and reunion are central, and the word 'brother' (אָח) appears prominently.

label: Renaming and Covenant
why: Exodus 39:1-29 emphasizes the crafting of Aaron's sacred garments, particularly the ephod and breastpiece, which are central to the covenantal role of the priesthood.

label: Family Expansion and Conflict
why: Deuteronomy 25:5-10 puts it this way, using יָבַם (to be brother-in-law) and יְבֵמֶת (sister-in-law), central to the levirate duty.

label: Jacob's grief and deception
why: Leviticus 18:25, 27, and 28 use this phrase to describe the land rejecting the wicked, which parallels Jacob's emotional rejection and grief over Joseph, as well as the motif of being cut off.

label: Joseph interprets dreams
why: The passages repeatedly use the verb פּתַר (to interpret) in the context of חֲלוֹם (dream), as seen in Genesis 40 and 41 where Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams.

label: Signs and miracles as proof
why: Exodus 4:2-9, Exodus 11:9-10, and Deuteronomy 11:2-7 use this phrase to describe the miraculous acts that prove God's power and presence.

label: Divine name and covenant
why: Exodus 6:2-3 and other passages use this phrase to reveal the divine name and its covenantal relationship with Israel.

label: Roles of Moses and Aaron
why: Exodus 7:1-2, 6, 15-16 and other passages repeatedly refer to Moses and Aaron as a pair, emphasizing their joint roles in God's plan.

label: Plagues and divine authority
why: Exodus 7:17-21, 10:4-15, and 10:21-23 show Moses as the one who sent the plagues as acts of divine authority.

label: Preparation for covenant
why: The passages emphasize the preparation of the people, the mountain, and the altar in anticipation of the covenant, using terms like כּוּן ('prepare') and בְּרִית ('covenant').

label: Divine presence and holiness
why: The term כָּבוֹד (glory) is central to passages describing God's presence and holiness, especially in Exodus and Leviticus, where it is associated with fire, vision, and awe.

label: Instructions for worship
gloss: to bring near to the Lord
why: Leviticus 16 and Numbers 15 use this phrase to describe the act of presenting offerings, central to the theme of worship and atonement.

label: Liability for Property and Animals
why: Exodus 21 and Deuteronomy 25 emphasize responsibility for animals (shor) and property (bayit), including the duties of the owner (ba'al) and compensation (natan).

label: Laws about marriage and seduction
why: Exodus 22:15-16 and Deuteronomy 21:10-14 both focus on laws involving women in specific marital states, particularly the בְּתוּלָה (unbetrothed woman), central to the theme of marriage and seduction laws.

label: Receiving the tablets of the covenant
why: Exodus 31:18 and Leviticus 10:12-15 both emphasize the act of receiving (לֶקַח) the tablets or portions as part of sacred service (לַעֲבֹדָה).

label: Moses' intercession and mercy
why: Exodus 32:11-14 and Deuteronomy 9:18-29 show Moses praying (פָּלַל) and God relenting (נָחַם) from destroying the people.

label: Consequences and punishment
why: Numbers 15:30-31 and Leviticus 24:23 describe being cut off from the people for defiant sins, and Exodus 32:26-29 shows Levites executing those who participated in idolatry, emphasizing communal exclusion as punishment.

label: Scapegoat and sin removal
why: Leviticus 16:8, 10, and 21 put it this way, naming the goat that bears the sins of the people away.

label: Prohibition of blood consumption
why: Leviticus 17:10-11, Deuteronomy 12:15-16 use this phrase to describe the prohibited act central to the theme.

label: Priestly inheritance and sustenance
why: The passages emphasize the Levites' and priests' inheritance through offerings and tithes, with 'נַחֲלָה' (inheritance) and 'כֹּהֵן' (priest) central to the theme.

label: Consequences of uncleanness
why: These words appear together in the context of uncleanness affecting individuals and the community, as in Numbers 19 and Deuteronomy 21.

label: Order and separation
why: Genesis 1:5, 8, 14-18 use this phrase to describe the separation and order between night and day, waters and waters, and the celestial lights, reflecting the theme of order and separation.

label: Instructions for building the ark
why: Genesis 6:14-21 centers on the command to build the ark, using תֵּבָה and עָשָׂה in the context of construction.

label: The flood begins
why: Genesis 7:10-12 describes the floodwaters covering the land, and 'רָחַץ' (to wash) is used in Exodus 30:17-21 in a related context of washing.

label: Moral responsibility and justice
why: Genesis 9:5-6 and Genesis 20:8-13, 15-16 both center on the moral weight of human life and the justice owed to it, using 'דָּם' (blood) and 'אָדָם' (man) to frame the ethical responsibility.

label: Canaanite clans and their territories
why: Genesis 10:15-19 and Deuteronomy 2:20-22 describe the clans and territories of the Canaanites, using the words מִשְׁפָּחָה (family) and כְּנַעֲנִי (Canaanite) to frame the theme.

label: covenant ratification through ritual
why: Exodus 24:8 explicitly mentions the covenant being ratified with blood, using the words בְּרִית (covenant) and דָּם (blood).

label: Marital and cultural concerns
why: The word 'אֵ֫לֶּה' (these) appears in passages addressing cultural and marital norms, such as in Genesis 27:46 and Deuteronomy 22:5.

label: Shechem's desire and proposal
why: Genesis 34:3-8 describes Shechem's emotional attachment and proposal to Dinah, using terms like שָׁכַב and אִשָּׁה, while Numbers 5:11-31 reflects marital fidelity and jealousy, tying to the theme of union and desire.

label: Establishing Sacred Places
why: Jacob refers to Bethel as 'the house of God' and 'the gate of heaven,' and the recurring use of מָקוֹם (place) with reference to God establishes sacred locations.

label: Genealogies of Esau
why: Genesis 36:1-19 lists the families and descendants of Esau, using language that aligns with this phrase.

label: Chieftains of Edom
why: Genesis 36:15-30, 40-43 lists the chieftains of Edom, using the word 'אַלּוּף' (chief) and 'אֱדוֹם' (Edom) repeatedly.

label: Joseph's dreams and his brothers' jealousy
why: Genesis 37:5-11 and 42:6-16 center on Joseph's dreams and his brothers' reactions, making this phrase a concise representation of the theme.

label: Joseph's betrayal and sale into slavery
gloss: a brother sells to his brother
why: Genesis 37:28 puts it this way as Joseph's brothers sell him to the Ishmaelites, capturing the betrayal and sale central to the theme.

label: Judah's Recognition of Righteousness
why: Genesis 38:26 puts Judah's acknowledgment of Tamar's righteousness at the center, and the Hebrew phrase captures the theme of moral reckoning and familial duty.

label: False Accusation and Consequences
why: Exodus 29 describes sacrificial slaughter for atonement, and Genesis 39 shows innocent slaughter by accusation, both using שָחַט and the theme of unjust taking.

label: Fate of the cupbearer and baker
why: Genesis 40:20-22 and 40:14-15 describe the fates of the cupbearer and the baker as interpreted and fulfilled by Joseph.

label: Moses' journey to Egypt
why: Exodus 4:18-21 and Deuteronomy 1:1-8 both describe Moses' journey to Egypt, using forms of הָלַךְ ('go') and מִצְרַיִם ('Egypt').

label: Circumcision and divine judgment
why: Exodus 4:24-26 connects the lack of circumcision (foreskin) with a life-threatening judgment (blood), making these terms central to the theme.

label: Frustration and divine response
why: Deuteronomy 8:2 and Exodus 5:23-24 show how God tested Israel in the wilderness, a central context for the theme of frustration and divine response.

label: Warning of future plagues
gloss: Tomorrow I will do a deed
why: Exodus 11:1-2, 4-8 uses this phrasing to announce a coming plague as a final warning before the Israelites' release.

label: Distinction between Israel and Egypt
why: Deuteronomy 12 emphasizes that God chose a specific place for worship, distinguishing Israel's devotion from Egyptian practices.

label: Moses' Leadership and Divine Instruction
why: Exodus 17:5 and Deuteronomy 20:2-4 show Moses receiving and delivering divine instruction, central to his leadership.

label: Moses' heavy workload
why: Exodus 18:14 and Numbers 11:12 both highlight Moses' solitary burden, using forms of בַּד ('alone') to emphasize his isolation in leadership.

label: Moses follows Jethro's advice
why: Exodus 18:24-27 and Numbers 1:4-16 both highlight Moses appointing or working with leaders from each tribe.

label: Limitations for safety and reverence
why: Exodus 19:12-13 and 24:15-18 emphasize the setting of boundaries around Mount Sinai to ensure reverence and safety in approaching God.

label: Servitude and Freedom
why: Leviticus 25 uses גְּאֻלָּה (redemption) and שׁוּב (return) to describe the restoration of freedom and property during the Jubilee, central to the theme of servitude and freedom.

label: Laws of Injury and Compensation
gloss: one who strikes a person and gives
why: Exodus 21:12-27 uses this structure to describe the act of causing harm and the obligation to provide compensation.

label: Appointment of artisans
why: Exodus 31:1-6 and 38:21-23 describe the appointment of artisans to perform the work of constructing the sanctuary.

label: Instructions for sacred construction
why: Exodus 31:7-11 lists the items to be made for the Tabernacle, including utensils for sacred use, and Numbers 10:33-36 references the sacred Ark and the presence of the LORD, emphasizing the holy items associated with divine service.

label: Divine covenant and rest
why: Exodus 31:17 directly links the Sabbath to God's rest, establishing it as a foundational theme.

label: The Tent of Meeting
why: Exodus 33:7-11 and Leviticus 8:31-35 both refer to the specific structure where God meets with Moses and the priests, using this exact phrase.

label: Festivals and Offerings
why: Leviticus 23 repeatedly uses מֹועָד (meeting/festival) and עֲבוֹדָה (service/work) to describe the structure and purpose of the festivals and their associated rituals.

label: Materials and measurements
why: Exodus 36:8-30 and 39:43 describe the making of the Tabernacle with specific materials and measurements.

label: Crafting the Lampstand
why: Exodus 37:17-23 describes the lampstand as being made by beating (מִקְשָׁה) a single piece of gold into its form.

label: Creation of the Incense Altar
why: Exodus 37:25-28 and Leviticus 16:11-16, 18-19, 33 refer to the altar specifically associated with the burning of incense, using this exact phrase.

label: High priestly duties
why: Leviticus 16 emphasizes the high priest's role in atoning in the sanctuary, especially on the Day of Atonement.

label: Use of Trumpets
why: Numbers 10:2-10 describes the use of trumpets for signals and calls to assembly, often linked with terua (shouting), while Deuteronomy 12 connects offerings with communal celebration and sound.

label: Moses and Hobab
why: The passages refer to Moses and Hobab directly, and the theme centers on their interaction and journey together.

label: Provision of quail and divine judgment
why: Numbers 11:31-33 and Deuteronomy 1:9-18 both feature the provision of quail and the establishment of judgment through divine command.

label: Moses' unique relationship with God
why: The passages emphasize Moses' singular, intimate relationship with God, and the Hebrew phrase 'מֹשֶׁה וְאֵלָהָיו' captures this unique bond as expressed in the text.

label: Divine punishment for speaking against Moses
why: Deuteronomy 3:26-27 describes how Moses was not allowed to pass into the land, and Numbers 12:10 implies a similar fate for Miriam for speaking against Moses.

label: Moses intercedes for Miriam
why: Numbers 12:9 and 12:15 describe the LORD being incensed at Miriam and Moses interceding to avert His anger, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Positive Assessment of the Land
gloss: land flowing with milk and honey
why: Numbers 13:27-28 describes the land in these exact words, and it is the central image of the positive assessment.

label: Punishment for rebellion
why: Numbers 17 describes a plague (נֶ֫גֶף) that kills rebels, and breaking the neck (עָרַף) is a form of execution associated with rebellion in the text.

label: Atonement and divine intervention
why: Numbers 17:11-13 describes Aaron making atonement with incense to stop the plague, capturing the central act of divine intervention and atonement in the theme.

label: Reminder of holiness and boundaries
why: The passages emphasize the altar as a central symbol of holiness and boundaries, particularly in Numbers 17 where the altar is overlaid as a reminder of consecration and divine order.

label: Levitical duties and priesthood roles
why: Numbers 18 emphasizes the Levitical service (מִשְׁמֶ֫רֶת) and the duties of the priesthood (כְּהֻנָּה) in relation to the sanctuary.

label: Aaron's Death and Transition of Leadership
gloss: Death of Aaron and the transfer of his garments
why: Numbers 20:22-29 and 33:38-39 describe Aaron's death on Mount Hor and the passing of his priestly garments to Eleazar, symbolizing the transition of leadership.

label: Military conquests
why: The passages describe Israel's wars with the Amorites, Midianites, and others, using terms like חָרַם (to devote) and שָׁבָה (to take captive), which are central to the theme of military conquests and the spoils or destruction that follow.

label: Vows and sacred naming
why: Numbers 30 and other passages use these terms to describe sacred commitments and naming.

label: Life and reproduction
why: Genesis 1:20-25 describes God creating living beings (חַיָּה) that swarm (שָׁרַץ) and reproduce, emphasizing multiplication and life.

label: Creation completed
why: Genesis 2:2-3 states that God completed his work (כָּלָה מְלָאכָה) and rested on the seventh day.

label: Duration of the flood
why: Genesis 7:24 refers to the flood and its duration on the earth.

label: The waters recede
why: Genesis 8:3 describes the waters receding and returning from off the earth.

label: Testing the earth with birds
why: Genesis 8:8-12 describes Noah sending out a dove to test the earth.

label: A covenant with the earth
why: Genesis 9:9-17 describes God's covenant with Noah, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood, using the words לֹא and עוֹד.

label: The sin and shame of Noah's son
why: Genesis 9:22 puts it this way, capturing the central act of shame and sin in the story.

label: Nimrod's rise to power
why: Genesis 10:8-12 describes Nimrod as a 'mighty hunter before the Lord,' and 'gibbor' (mighty) is central to his characterization.

label: Abram's return and prosperity
why: Genesis 13:1 describes Abram returning from Egypt to Canaan, making 'שׁוּב אַבְרָם' (shuv Avram) the most fitting phrase for the theme of his return and subsequent prosperity.

label: refusal of worldly gain
gloss: I will not take what is yours
why: Genesis 14:22-23 puts Abram's refusal in these terms, rejecting wealth from Sodom's king.

label: covenant sign through circumcision
why: Genesis 17:10-11, 13 refer to the covenant established through the sign of circumcision.

label: renaming as covenant symbol
why: Genesis 17:5 and 17:15 describe God giving new names (שֵׁם) to Abram and Sarai, signifying a covenantal change.

label: Deception and blessings
gloss: Blessed Esau and gave it to Jacob
why: Genesis 27:29 captures the central irony of the theme: the blessing meant for Esau is given to Jacob through deception.

label: Fear and protective planning
why: Rebekah uses this imperative to Jacob as she urges him to flee for his life, forming the core of her protective planning.

label: Mission and journey for marriage
gloss: to take a wife from the family
why: This phrase captures the central action and motivation in the passages, particularly Genesis 28:1-2 and 29:10-12, where Jacob is sent to Paddan-aram to take a wife from his extended family.

label: Meeting and love for a spouse
why: Genesis 29:1-12 describes Jacob meeting Rachel at the well, where he waters the flock, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Work for marriage
why: Genesis 29:15-20 describes Jacob serving Laban for seven years in exchange for Rachel.

label: Deception in marriage
why: Genesis 29:25 puts it this way, describing how Laban deceived Jacob by making Leah his wife instead of Rachel.

label: Extended labor for marriage
why: Genesis 29:27-28 describes Jacob working two additional weeks for Rachel after marrying Leah.

label: Fertility and barrenness
why: Genesis 29:31-35 repeatedly contrasts Leah's ability to conceive and bear children with Rachel's barrenness, using the words הָרָה and בֵּן.

label: Divine intervention in family
why: This phrase captures the central divine action in the passages, particularly in Genesis 30:22-24, where God opens Rachel’s womb and answers the prayers of Leah and Rachel regarding childbearing.

label: Prosperity and separation of assets
why: Genesis 30:32-43 describes Jacob separating his flocks from Laban's using a system of striped and spotted livestock, which the text calls פָּצַל צֹאן ('peeled flock') to describe the distinct grouping.

label: Symbolic exchange and rivalry
why: Genesis 30:15-16 uses this phrase to describe the exchange of mandrakes for conjugal rights, central to the rivalry between Rachel and Leah.

label: Departure and divine guidance
why: Genesis 30 and 31 describe Jacob's management of Laban's flock, particularly his focus on the speckled and spotted animals as part of his divine guidance and departure.

label: Loyalty and acknowledgment of injustice
gloss: for our father said to us
why: This phrase captures the acknowledgment of injustice and loyalty to family, as seen in Genesis 31:14-16 where Rachel and Leah reference their father Laban's actions.

label: Journey and confrontation
why: Genesis 31:20, 21, and 27 describe Jacob fleeing from Laban, which initiates the journey and confrontation theme.

label: Covenant and peace agreement
why: Genesis 31:43-53 describes Jacob and Laban setting up a heap of stones as a witness to their covenant, using the words גַּל (heap) and עֵד (witness).

label: Justification and grievance
why: Jacob uses this phrase in Genesis 31:36-42 to express his sense of grievance and self-justification in the face of Laban’s treatment.

label: Fear and anticipation of reunion
why: The passages focus on the tension and anticipation between Jacob and Esau, particularly in Genesis 32 where Jacob fears Esau's approach and prepares for their reunion.

label: Preparation for reconciliation
why: Genesis 32:20 describes Jacob sending a gift to Esau, his brother, as an act of reconciliation.

label: Divine struggle and transformation
why: Genesis 32:30 puts it this way, after Jacob wrestles with a divine being at Peniel and acknowledges his encounter with God.

label: Divine presence and division
why: Genesis 32:1-3 describes Jacob encountering divine messengers at a place he names, emphasizing the presence of God in a specific location.

label: Order and deference
why: Genesis 33:8-10 describes Jacob seeking to find favor in Esau's eyes through deference and gifts.

label: Family organization and identity
why: Genesis 33 emphasizes Jacob's family (מִשְׁפֶּחַ֥ה) and the recognition of his children and their identities (שֵׁ֖ם), especially in the context of reuniting with Esau.

label: Acknowledgment of divine favor
why: Genesis 33:5, 10-11 reflect Jacob's acknowledgment of receiving divine favor and grace.

label: Jacob's sons' anger and conditions
why: Genesis 34:14-17 shows Jacob's sons demanding that the men of Shechem be circumcised as a condition for marriage, framing it as a covenant.

label: The circumcision and betrayal
why: Genesis 34:24-25 describes the men of Shechem being circumcised and then being killed by Jacob's sons.

label: Plunder and Jacob's reaction
why: Genesis 34:27-30 describes Jacob's sons plundering the city and its people, and the phrase captures the action (plunder) and its target (household and city).

label: Separation from Jacob
why: Genesis 36:6-8 describes Esau's migration due to their large possessions, with 'יָשַׁב' (to dwell) and 'מִקְנֶה' (livestock) central to the narrative.

label: Kings of Edom
why: Genesis 36:31-39 lists the succession of rulers in Edom, using the phrase מַלְכֵּי אֱדוֹם ('kings of Edom').

label: Reuben's attempt to save Joseph
why: Genesis 37:22 and 37:30 refer to Reuben's attempt to rescue Joseph from the pit, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Judah's Wicked Sons
why: Genesis 38:8-9 puts it this way as Judah instructs Onan to fulfill the levirate duty by fathering a child with his brother's widow.

label: Tamar's Deception
why: Genesis 38:14-18 describes Tamar's act of disguising herself, which can be interpreted as covering or concealing her identity and the way she approached Judah.

label: The Birth of Perez and Zerah
gloss: he begat two sons who came out
why: Genesis 38:27-30 describes the birth of Perez and Zerah, using יָלַד ('beget'), יָצָא ('come out'), and שְׁנֵי בָנִים ('two sons').

label: Divine Favor and Success
why: The passages emphasize how Joseph receives divine favor (חֵן) and experiences prosperity (צָלֵחַ) in Egypt, especially in the house of his master.

label: Moral Integrity and Temptation
gloss: I will not do the thing
why: Genesis 39:8-9, where Joseph refuses his master's wife's advances, declaring this phrase to affirm his moral integrity.

label: Divine purpose in Joseph's suffering
why: Genesis 45:5-8 reflects on how Joseph's suffering was part of God's plan, aligning with the concept of divine purpose expressed in the text.

label: Leadership and divine reassurance
gloss: I am the one who goes out
why: Exodus 3:12 uses a form of these words to express God's assurance to Moses that He will accompany him in leading Israel out of Egypt.

label: Pharaoh's resistance to God
why: Exodus 5:2-5 shows Pharaoh's refusal to let the people go, using the verb הָלַךְ (to go) in the negative.

label: Oppression and resistance
why: Exodus 5:6-18 describes Pharaoh's oppressive measures against the Israelite people, using the word נָגַשׂ ('to oppress') and referring to the עַם ('people').

label: Preparation for confrontation
gloss: The LORD our fathers' God sends us
why: Exodus 6:26-29 and related passages frame Moses and Aaron's mission as a divine sending to confront Pharaoh, using language like 'YHWH' and 'meshal'cheinu' (he sends us).

label: Defiance and divine threat
why: Exodus 7:14, 22, 26-29 show Pharaoh's hardened heart and defiance, central to the theme of resistance to divine command and threat.

label: God's Judgment
why: Isaiah 1:5-8, 8:7-8, and 17:4-6 use this imagery to describe divine judgment as a sword falling upon the land, bringing desolation and destruction.

label: God's ultimate sovereignty and redemption
why: This phrase appears in passages that emphasize God's ultimate authority and redemptive role, especially in relation to the land and covenant with Israel.

label: Divine Deception
why: The passages in Proverbs repeatedly contrast folly (סִכְלוּת) with wisdom (חׇכְמָה), framing the theme around the tension between these two opposing forces.

label: Rejection of Ritual
why: Isaiah 1:11-15 and 66:3-4 emphasize the futility (שָׁוְא) of empty rituals and offerings (שֵׁבֶל), which are rejected by God.

label: Symbolic vision and divine judgment
why: The passages in Daniel and Jeremiah repeatedly use symbolic visions to convey divine judgment, with words like חָז֛וֹן (vision) and מִשְׁפָּט (judgment) central to the theme.

label: Promise of Restoration
why: Isaiah 14:1-3 and 52:1-9 express the restoration of Israel through return and rejoining, using שׁוֹבָב ('turning back') and לָוָה ('to join').

label: Future glory of Zion
why: Isaiah 60:1-22 and 62:1-4 describe the future glory and exaltation of Zion, using language that reflects its rising to prominence and being honored among nations.

label: afterlife and divine justice
why: Luke 20:34-36 and other passages emphasize the nature of life after death as distinct from earthly existence, using language that implies an eternal, ageless state.

label: God's faithfulness and justice
why: These passages emphasize God's unwavering commitment to justice (מִשְׁפָּט) and righteousness (צְדָקָה), particularly in His covenant faithfulness and moral governance over Israel and humanity.

label: Righteousness and blessed life
why: Psalms 1, 104-108 emphasize the blessed life through God's righteousness (צֶדֶק) and His steadfast kindness (חֶסֶד), which are central to the theme.

label: Call to Repentance
why: The passages in Isaiah repeatedly use forms of נָחַם (to be sorry, comfort) and חֵטְא (sin), and the call to return to God is central, as in Isaiah 55:7: 'Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return

label: Day of the Lord
why: This phrase is used in passages like Joel 3:3-4, Amos 5:18-20, and Zechariah 14:1-3 to describe a time of divine judgment and cosmic upheaval.

label: Return to God
why: Deuteronomy 30:2-10 and other passages use forms of שׁוּב ('return') in the context of turning back to God, making it central to the theme.

label: Military confrontation and divine intervention
why: The passages repeatedly describe battles (מִלְחָמָה) where divine intervention (עֵזְרַת אֱלֹהִים) is central to victory, as seen in 1 Chronicles 14, 18–20 and 2 Kings 6.

label: Discovery and Greed
why: The passages repeatedly contrast the fates and behaviors of the wicked and the righteous, framing the theme around their opposing paths and outcomes.

label: Call and response in love
why: Isaiah 10 and 13-14 use this dynamic of divine action and human or national response, while Song of Songs 8:13-14 reflects a personal call and response in love.

label: Organization of the Camps
why: The passages in 1 Chronicles 12 and 23, and others, use terms like מִשְׁמֶרֶת (division) and צָבָא (army) to describe organized groups within military or tribal structures.

label: Failure of the Spies
why: Numbers 14:36-37 and Joshua 14:6-12 highlight the refusal and consequences of the spies' report, with מֵאֵן (refusing) being central to the theme.

label: anointing and legitimacy
why: The passages repeatedly use 'מָשַׁח' (to anoint) and 'מֶ֫לֶךְ' (king) to describe the legitimacy and divine appointment of rulers such as Solomon, Joash, and David.

label: Judah's Rebellion
why: Jeremiah 8:11 and 9:10-16 use these terms to describe the judgment and destruction of Judah due to their rebellion.

label: Watchfulness and Readiness
gloss: to keep watch and be watchful
why: The passages in Mark 13:33-37 and Matthew 24:42-44 use these terms to emphasize the need for constant readiness and alertness for Jesus' return.

label: Cyclical Pattern of Sin and Rescue
why: This phrase captures the cyclical pattern of sin and rescue found in Judges 2:16-19, Psalms 78:8-22, and Psalms 95:8-11, where Israel repeatedly sins, faces divine anger, and is rescued or called to repentance.

label: Yahweh's fulfillment of promises
gloss: Yahweh gave the land as He spoke
why: Joshua 21:43-45 and Psalm 44:2-4 directly affirm that Yahweh fulfilled His promises by giving Israel the land.

label: Israel's disobedience to God
why: Isaiah 5:1-7 and Isaiah 43:22-28 use 'ma'alah' (deed) and 'avon' (iniquity) to describe Israel's disobedient actions toward God.

label: Choice between life and death
why: Deuteronomy 30:15-19 presents the choice in these exact terms, framing the central theme of the passages.

label: Missionary outreach and church growth
why: Passages like Acts 11:19-26 and Acts 18:7-8 show the spread of the gospel and church growth as fulfilling the command to make disciples.

label: Loyalty and covenant in friendship
why: The passages emphasize loyalty and covenant in friendship, particularly in 1 Samuel where Jonathan and David affirm their bond before God, and 'berit' (covenant) and 'ahava' (love) are central to the language of their commitment.

label: recognition and divine wisdom
why: The passages emphasize recognizing divine wisdom through truth (emet) and reflection (hagah), especially in the context of judgment and righteousness.

label: Divine Knowledge and Human Responsibility
why: Ecclesiastes and Proverbs emphasize the limits of human knowledge (דּעַת) and the burden of understanding (מַחֲשָׁבָה), while Deuteronomy and Psalms contrast divine insight with human responsibility.

label: loyalty and devotion in marriage
why: The motif of close, faithful presence—such as Ruth lying at Boaz’s feet or David and Jonathan’s covenantal bond—is captured in the phrase 'to see foot,' which appears in the language of proximity and loyalty in these passages.

label: Massacre and divine injustice
why: The phrase encapsulates the recurring motif of violence against divine representatives (priests, kings) and the seeming injustice in their slaughter, as seen in the deaths of Ahimelech, Saul, and others.

label: divine presence and covenant
why: This phrase captures the divine presence and covenantal commitment, as seen in passages like 1 Kings 6:11-13 and Haggai 2:4-5, where God promises to dwell among His people and remain with them.

label: Conflict with Amalek
why: Exodus 17:8-13 describes the conflict between Israel and the Amalekites, and 'עֲמָלֵק' (Amalek) is central to the theme.

label: rise of a prophet
why: The passages repeatedly describe individuals chosen by God to speak on His behalf, using the term 'prophet' (נָבִיא) and emphasizing their relationship with 'the Lord' (יְהֹוָה).

label: Divine protection from enemies
why: This phrase captures the core idea of divine protection from enemies, as seen in passages like 2 Samuel 22 and Psalms 107, where God rescues from distress (מִצַּר) and delivers from danger.

label: temple construction
why: 1 Kings 6:1-38, 2 Chronicles 3:1-17, and Ezra 1:1-4 describe the construction of the temple as 'bayit' (house) and 'heikhal' (temple), the two most central terms for the structure.

label: Prophetic succession and calling
why: The phrase captures the idea of succession and calling, as seen in 1 Kings 19:19-21 (Elijah to Elisha) and the recurring motif of one prophet preparing the way for another.

label: Divine Judgment on Hazael
why: 2 Kings 8:15 and 12:18-19 refer to the conclusion of Hazael's reign and its impact on Israel.

label: Hope for Restoration
why: The passages repeatedly express longing for Zion's return to glory, using terms like restoration, renewal, and flourishing, with צִיּוֹן (Zion) and שׁוּב (to return) central to the theme.

label: Divine judgment and separation
why: The phrase encapsulates the divine action of judgment and separation, as seen in Numbers 16 and Judges 2, where God acts in judgment against rebellion and unfaithfulness.

label: kinsman and community responsibilities
why: The passages emphasize the responsibilities of close relatives and community leaders, as seen in the roles of Ammiel and Zedekiah, and the broader themes in Ruth and Jeremiah.

label: Loyalty and divine favor in adversity
why: The passages highlight loyalty (chesed) and divine favor through the actions of individuals like David, Abner, Jehu, and Joash, who are positioned as servants (avad) of God amid adversity.

label: temple preparation
gloss: build a house for the LORD
why: 1 Kings 5:15-20, 1 Chronicles 22:1-16, and Psalms 132:1-5 all use forms of בָּנָה (to build) in the context of preparing a temple for the LORD.

label: Lament and divine anger
why: The passages use נְהִי (wailing) and עִזָּבוֹן (abandonment) to express the emotional and divine themes of lament and divine anger.

label: Sacred offerings and their distribution
why: The terms תְּרוּמָה (contribution) and מַעֲשֵׂר (tithe) appear prominently in passages detailing sacred offerings and their distribution, especially in Numbers 18 and 2 Chronicles 31.

label: Joshua's leadership and Moses' legacy
why: This phrase captures the transition of leadership from Moses to Joshua (Deuteronomy 34:9-12; Joshua 1:1-2) and is extended thematically to David receiving leadership and legacy (2 Samuel 19:12-40), with the word קָבַל (to receive) and מֶ֫לֶ

label: Lineage of David
why: The passages emphasize the royal lineage and covenant promises to David, particularly in 2 Samuel 23, 1 Chronicles 17, and Psalms 89, which focus on the enduring kingship of David's descendants.

label: Divine transformation and prophecy
why: The theme is centered on prophecy and divine transformation, and the word 'נָבָא' (to prophesy) appears in key passages like 1 Samuel 19:22-24, where Saul is overcome by the spirit and begins to prophesy.

label: wisdom and justice
why: Psalms 45:8 and Proverbs 28:5-7 emphasize wisdom and justice as central to righteous living, while 1 Kings 3:16-27 illustrates wisdom in action to achieve just outcomes.

label: labor and logistics
why: The passages emphasize organized labor, resource management, and dedicated effort, often linked to temple-building or divine service, as seen in 1 Kings 5, 2 Chronicles 2, and Luke 1.

label: Healing and resurrection
why: This phrase captures the core of the theme as seen in passages like Luke 7:11-16 and 2 Kings 4:18-37, where Jesus and Elisha restore life to the dead, a central motif in the text.

label: Sending tribes to their inheritance
why: Joshua 22:9 and Nehemiah 11:1-36 emphasize the sending of tribes to their inheritance and the settling of leaders and families in their allotted places.

label: Rivalry and persecution between kings
why: The passages repeatedly feature rebellion (מְרִי) against rulers and messengers (מַלְאָךְ) sent to confront or warn kings, especially in 1 Kings 20, 2 Kings 1, and Jeremiah 20.

label: Oath and covenant in loyalty
why: Psalms 94:3-7, Proverbs 28-29, and Isaiah 5 put the contrast between the righteous and the wicked at the heart of the theme, showing how loyalty to covenant and oath separates them.

label: divine wisdom and governance
why: 1 Kings 3:5-14 and Psalms 72:1-4, 99:4 emphasize divine wisdom (חָכְמָה) and justice (מִשְׁפָּט) as central to righteous governance.

label: Paul's apostleship and the gospel
why: This phrase captures the central theme of Paul's self-identification and mission, as seen in passages like Romans 1:1 and Ephesians 3:8-9.

label: Warning Against Apostasy
gloss: Do not act foolishly before God
why: Ecclesiastes 5:1-6 and 10:11-15, 20 emphasize the consequences of foolish speech and actions before God, aligning with the theme of warning against apostasy.

label: growth and divine dedication
why: The passages emphasize the covenant between God and His people and the importance of adhering to divine instruction, as seen in Jeremiah 1:10 and Ezekiel 44:6-8.

label: Legal and social order in governance
why: This phrase captures the recurring concern with just governance and the moral responsibilities of leaders, as seen in Proverbs 28 and 29, where mishpat (justice) and tsadiq (righteous) are central to the critique and ideal of leadership.

label: Call to justice and strength
why: Ecclesiastes 9:11-12 and 1:2, 14 put it this way, emphasizing the unpredictability and futility of human striving under the sun.

label: Universal judgment and divine sovereignty
why: Revelation 7:1-3 and 9:4 emphasize the sealing of God's servants as a mark of divine protection and sovereignty over life and judgment.

label: Jesus' betrayal and arrest
why: Matthew 26:14-16, 47-50 and Luke 22:3-6 use these terms to describe Judas's betrayal of Jesus.

label: The universality of the gospel
why: This phrase captures the central theme of the universality of the gospel, as seen in passages like Romans 1:5-15 and Ephesians 3:3-6, where the gospel's reach to Gentiles and all nations is emphasized.

label: Spiritual gifts and their source
why: The passages emphasize the role of the Spirit as the source and power behind spiritual gifts and Christian living, especially in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, Ephesians 3:14-19, and Ephesians 5:18-21.

label: God as the Source of Comfort
why: 2 Corinthians 1:3-7 puts it this way, calling God 'the Father of mercies and God of all comfort'.

label: Feminine heroism and prophecy
why: Judges 4:17-22 and Song of Songs 2:7, 3:5 use imagery of women as active, protective, and central to divine or moral action, while εὐφραίνω and σπλαγχνίζομαι in Luke 10 and 15 highlight emotional and moral depth in women.

label: answered prayer and child dedication
why: 1 Samuel 1:19-28 shows Hannah asking (שָׁאַל) for a child and giving (וַיִּתֶּן) Samuel to God.

label: Emotional response and acknowledgment of righteousness
why: Ecclesiastes 2:24, 3:12-13, and 5:19 emphasize finding joy in life's gifts and God's good provision, while 1 Samuel 24:17-21 and Jonah 4:6-8 show emotional response to righteousness and divine compassion.

label: governance and administration
gloss: to give a face to an order
why: This phrase captures the essence of governance and administration as seen in passages like 1 Kings 4 and 1 Chronicles 22, where assigning roles and responsibilities (orders) to individuals (faces) is central.

label: Prophetic succession and divine transition
why: The passages highlight transitions in prophetic leadership (Elijah to Elisha, John the Baptist) and shifts in priestly roles (Melchizedek order, temple reforms), using terms like 'priesthood' and names of prophets to mark divine succession.

label: Jewish identity and royal selection
why: Ezekiel 48:1-29 and other passages use these terms to describe the division of land among the tribes, central to Jewish identity and royal selection.

label: Warning against moral failure
why: Psalms 50:16-22 and Psalms 52:2-6 put it this way, emphasizing the warning against moral failure through deceit and wickedness.

label: Restoration and blessing
why: Luke 15:20-24, 3 John 1:3-4, and Revelation 5:8-12 all use forms of 'to rejoice' (χαίρω, εὐφραίνω) and 'to sacrifice' (θυσία) to express restoration and blessing through celebration and divine favor.

label: Judgment on idolatry and pride
why: Ezekiel 23 and 28, along with Isaiah 2 and Jeremiah 51, repeatedly use these terms to describe the sins of idolatry and pride that lead to divine judgment.

label: Return of the Son of Man
gloss: Return of the Son of Man
why: Mark 13:24-27 and Matthew 24:29-31 describe the return of the Son of Man in power and glory, using this exact phrase.

label: Jesus' resurrection
gloss: he was raised from the dead
why: This phrase captures the central event described in the passages, particularly in Matthew 28:5-7, Mark 16:6, Luke 24:5-7, and John 20:1-18, where the angel or Jesus himself declares his resurrection.

label: Jesus' healing and compassion
why: This phrase captures the authoritative and compassionate language Jesus uses in healing (e.g., Mark 1:41, Luke 5:17-26), combining divine command (ἐπιτιμῶ) with the result of healing (ἀπόλυσις γίνεσθε).

label: Renewed Covenant
why: Exodus 34 and Hebrews 2-5 use forms of כָּרַת (to cut/make covenant) and emphasize renewal, while the New Testament passages highlight a new covenant in Christ.

label: Moses' humility and vision for others
why: Numbers 11:26-29 highlights Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp, and Moses' desire for all to be filled with the spirit; נָבָא and רוּחַ are central to the theme of shared vision and humility.

label: Divine punishment and repentance
why: 1 Corinthians 10-11 uses 'cup' (ποτήριον) and 'body' (σῶμα) to frame the Lord's Supper as a communal act of remembrance and judgment, central to the theme of divine punishment and repentance.

label: God's refusal to allow Balaam to curse Israel
why: Numbers 22:12 and 18 show God explicitly telling Balaam not to curse Israel, using this exact phrasing.

label: Parables and warnings
why: Matthew 13:3-35 and other passages use παραβολή (parable) and βασιλεύα (kingdom) to frame the central teaching method and theme of Jesus' warnings and teachings.

label: corruption of priestly sons
why: 1 Samuel 2:12-17 and Micah 6:9-12 use this term to describe the moral and spiritual corruption of the priestly sons and the people's wickedness.

label: Escape and protection of the innocent
gloss: entrance to life — highway for the righteous
why: These passages emphasize escape from danger, divine protection, and righteous deliverance, often through a turning or passage (סָבַב, διαπέρχομαι, σπεῖδω), with a focus on the righteous or innocent being saved (Zacchaeus, Abiathar, etc.).

label: securing succession
why: Isaiah 22:22-23 uses the metaphor of a peg to describe the secure authority of a steward, and the theme of securing succession is central to passages involving kings and their heirs.

label: rebellion and execution
why: The passages highlight rebellion (שָׁבַ֥ע, to return/refuse) and execution (צָבָ֖א, army/war), especially in the context of royal conspiracies and divine judgment.

label: alliance and cooperation
why: The passages involving David, Solomon, and Hiram of Tyre use כָּרַת (to cut) and בְּרִית (covenant) to describe the formation of alliances and cooperative agreements.

label: faith and recognition of God
why: Psalms 28:8 and 2 Chronicles 26:6-15 use these terms to describe God's strength and power in providing, protecting, and empowering.

label: brotherly unity
why: Psalms 133:1 declares the goodness of brothers living together in unity, and the theme is central to passages calling for love, shared faith, and reverence among believers and people of God.

label: desire for vengeance
why: Psalms 137:8-9 put it this way, expressing a desire for retribution and ruin upon Babylon.

label: Hope in divine salvation
why: Isaiah 2:18-21 and Isaiah 9:1-2 emphasize the exaltation of the Lord and the coming light of salvation, with הָדָר (glory) central to the hope in divine salvation.

label: Last Supper and Eucharist
why: Matthew 26:17-30, Mark 14:12-16, and Luke 22:7-20 all describe Jesus sharing the Passover meal with his disciples, which is central to the Last Supper and Eucharist.

label: Persecution of the church
why: This phrase captures the core conflict in passages like Acts 16:19-24 and Acts 18:12-17, where Paul and his companions are accused of causing public disturbance, leading to their arrest and persecution.

label: Greetings and final blessings
why: This phrase captures the essence of greetings and final blessings in the New Testament, particularly in passages like 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 13, where rejoicing (χαίρω), togetherness (σύν), and love (ἀγάπη) are central.

label: Reliability of God's Promises
why: Passages like 2 Corinthians 1:17-20 and Titus 3:3-7 emphasize the consistent and reliable nature of God's promises, especially salvation, which is always grounded in Christ.

label: Divine Memory and Eternal Conflict
why: The passages repeatedly emphasize divine intervention in conflict (e.g., Exodus 17:16, 1 Samuel 7:10-11, Psalms 110:5-6), and 'Mizpah' (מִצְפָּה) means 'watch' or 'watchtower,' symbolizing God's active presence and judgment in battle.

label: Commandment to keep the Sabbath
why: Exodus 31:12-17 puts it this way, emphasizing the Sabbath as a sign to be kept.

label: Excess offerings
why: Ezekiel 42:15-20 and 45:11-16 emphasize the act of measuring the temple complex and its surrounding areas, using the words מָדַד and סָבִיב repeatedly.

label: Fear and despair among the people
why: The passages repeatedly use 'נֶ֫פֶשׁ' (soul) and 'בָּהַל' (to dismay) to describe the inner turmoil and fear among the people.

label: Levitical cities and pasturelands
why: Joshua 21:1-41 and 1 Chronicles 6:39-66 repeatedly use these terms to describe the Levitical inheritance.

label: mistaken assumptions and prayer clarification
why: 1 Samuel 1:12-16 shows Eli's mistaken assumption and Hannah's clarifying prayer, and the theme is further reflected in other passages involving prayer and correction.

label: prayer of gratitude and divine justice
why: Luke 1:68-79 and Luke 2:25-38 use forms of ἐπισκ看法σις (to visit/care for) and highlight divine love and redemption, while gratitude and justice are implied in the fulfillment of God's promises.

label: divine power over false gods
why: This phrase captures the motif of divine power causing false gods or their representatives to be stripped of dignity and fall, as seen in the Philistine gods Dagon (1 Samuel 5) and the fate of Saul (1 Chronicles 10).

label: Reunion and emotional connection
why: 1 Samuel 20:35-41 captures the reunion and emotional connection between David and Jonathan, with שׁוּב (return) and אָוָה (desire) representing the longing and restoration of their bond.

label: Evasion and refuge from persecution
why: The passages repeatedly describe David evading those who pursue him, particularly Saul and the Philistines, and emphasize the hostility and danger posed by the wicked (רְשָׁעִים).

label: death and succession
gloss: to lie down, to bury, and the remainder reigns
why: These passages repeatedly use forms of שָׁכַב (to lie down/dead), קָבַר (to bury), and יֶ֫תֶר (remainder/successor) in the context of royal death and succession.

label: Lament over God's Anger and Neglect
why: The lament over God's anger and neglect is powerfully expressed in passages like Lamentations 5:18-20, where the desolation of Mount Zion and the sense of divine abandonment are central, and fire (אֵשׁ) is a recurring image of divine judgme

label: Pilgrimage and divine guidance
why: The passages in Isaiah 12 and Psalms 84 emphasize the journey of faith marked by giving thanks (יָדָה) and trusting in divine salvation (יְשׁוּעָה), reflecting the movement of pilgrimage and guidance.

label: Nature and fertility imagery
why: The theme is expressed through imagery of nature and fertility, with the 'door' symbolizing access and the 'glory' representing divine revelation, as in 2 Corinthians 4:6 and Colossians 1:24-27.

label: Jesus' suffering and obedience
why: The passages in Mark and Matthew emphasize Jesus' anguish and submission to the Father's will, encapsulated in the combination of suffering (πάσχων) and obedience (ὑποτασσόμενος).

label: Jesus' trial and condemnation
why: Matthew 27:23-24 and John 19:4-6 show Pilate declaring Jesus innocent and yielding to the crowd's demand to release Barabbas instead.

label: Crucifixion and death of Jesus
why: The crucifixion of Jesus is described in the Gospel passages using the verb σταυρῴω (to crucify), and the participle σταυρώσας captures the completed action central to the theme.

label: Conflict over Sabbath healing
why: This phrase captures the central conflict in passages like Mark 3:1-6, Luke 13:10-17, and John 5:10-18, where Jesus heals on the Sabbath, challenging religious interpretations of Sabbath law.

label: Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus
why: Acts 26:12-15 and 2 Corinthians 12:1-2 describe Paul's transformative vision on the road to Damascus, where he is seized by a revelation from Jesus.

label: Unity in diversity within the body of Christ
why: Ephesians 4:4 and 1 Corinthians 12:12-13 emphasize the unity of believers as one body under one Lord, central to the theme of unity in diversity.

label: Priestly appearance and mourning
why: Ezekiel 44:17-25 emphasizes the inner holiness of the priests, detailing their sacred conduct and separation, while the theme of mourning and priestly appearance reflects the tension between human emotion and divine holiness.

label: Leadership shared through elders
why: The term 'elders of Israel' appears in passages like 2 Chronicles 5:2-3 and Numbers 11:16-25, where leaders are gathered to share in governance and spiritual leadership.

label: Caleb's Encouragement
why: Caleb's central message in Numbers 13:30 is to trust in God and take possession of the land, using the verb שָמַר ('guard, keep') and the noun אֶ֫רֶץ ('land').

label: Consequences of unauthorized access
why: This phrase captures the central concern of the passages, particularly Numbers 18 and Isaiah 52, which emphasize the sacred duty of guarding and handling holy things, with consequences for unauthorized access.

label: Israel's threat to Moab
why: The word 'geder' (wall) appears in Numbers 22:4 as part of the description of Israel's encampment near Moab, symbolizing the boundary and threat posed by Israel.

label: Covenant and future disobedience
why: Deuteronomy 31 and Jeremiah 22-24 repeatedly frame the covenant (בְּרִית) alongside the people's disobedience and sin (עָוֹן), showing how breaking the covenant leads to divine judgment.

label: Legal protection and justice
why: Joshua 20:6 specifies the city of refuge as a place of legal protection until the death of the high priest.

label: Reconciliation and acceptance
why: Joshua 22 and Judges 5 use these terms to describe the resolution of tribal conflict and the reintegration of divided groups.

label: Public covenant and witness
why: The passages emphasize the people's public choice to enter into or uphold the covenant with God, as seen in Joshua 24 and 1 Kings 12.

label: prayer and vow to God for a child
gloss: to give thanks and speak to the LORD
why: Isaiah 38:15-20 and 1 Samuel 1:11 show Hezekiah and Hannah giving thanks and making vows to the LORD, expressing trust and devotion.

label: Military Defeat
why: 1 Kings 22:3, 23, 34 put it this way, describing the disastrous war at Ramoth Gilead manipulated by a lying spirit.

label: Consequences of improper handling of sacred objects
why: The theme is centered on the ark being struck, as in 1 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles 13, where improper handling leads to divine judgment.

label: Disguise and survival in enemy territory
gloss: watchfulness and survival in enemy land
why: The passages highlight strategies of concealment (e.g., pretending madness, denial), survival (e.g., fleeing to Gath), and navigating hostile environments (e.g., Herod's court, Peter's denial), all in the context of enemy territory.

label: Conflict and insult in negotiation
why: Passages like Job 8-9 and Micah 6:6-8 center on the conflict between divine justice (מִשְׁפָּט) and human wrongdoing (פֶּשַׁע), especially in the context of negotiation and response to insult.

label: census and divine retribution
why: 2 Samuel 24 uses מִסְפָּר for 'census' and עָוֺן for 'iniquity' and its consequences, central to the theme.

label: justice and execution
why: This phrase captures the violent execution motif in passages like 1 Kings 2:34, where Joab 'fell on the sword,' and reflects the broader theme of divine justice carried out through the sword, as in Ezekiel 30.

label: reign and wealth
why: The passages emphasize both the reign of kings like Solomon and the vast wealth and trade (e.g., מַעֲרָב, סָחַר, רָכַל) associated with their rule.

label: hypocrisy and punishment
why: 2 Kings 5:20-27 tells of Gehazi's deceit and punishment, using the words גֵּיחֲזִי and בֶּ֫גֶד to frame the theme of hypocrisy and its consequences.

label: Reinforcing patriarchal authority
why: The passages emphasize the role of rulers (מָשַׁל) and their visible authority (פָּנִים), reflecting how leadership is expressed through appearance and action.

label: Repentance and humility
why: The passages emphasize μετανοία (repentance) and the call to humble oneself before God, as seen in James 4:6-10 and 2 Corinthians 7:8-10.

label: Call to worship God joyfully
gloss: Sing to the Lord a new song
why: This phrase captures the exhortation to joyful worship found in passages like Psalms 81, 95, 98, and echoed in the call to rejoice in the Lord in Philippians.

label: God's covenant with Israel
why: The phrase encapsulates the recurring emphasis on God's enduring covenant with Israel, as seen in passages like Jeremiah 11 and 2 Corinthians 4.

label: Moral failure and ignorance
why: This phrase captures the theme of moral failure and ignorance as seen in passages like Psalms 82:5 and Proverbs 30:11-14, where the wicked walk in darkness or in ways that reflect injustice and lack of understanding.

label: God's forgiveness and mercy
why: Psalms 85:2-4, Isaiah 54:4-10, and Lamentations 3:21-24 all emphasize God's compassion (רַחֲמִים) and steadfast kindness (חֶ֫סֶד) in forgiving and not forsaking His people.

label: Power and permanence of love
why: The passages emphasize the enduring and unbreakable nature of love, especially in relationships and roles, as seen in Song of Songs 8:6-7 and 1 Timothy 2:13-14.

label: Call to repentance and faith
why: Ezekiel 18:30-32 emphasizes turning from transgression and returning to the Lord, central to the theme of repentance and faith.

label: calling nations to witness
why: Isaiah 18:3, Isaiah 24:15, and Micah 4:11-12 use this phrase to describe the calling of nations to witness divine action.

label: Kingdom of Heaven as a forceful pursuit
why: Matthew 11:12 puts it this way, and it is central to the theme of the forceful pursuit of divine rule.

label: Preparedness for the bridegroom
why: Matthew 25:1-13 uses these terms to describe the wise virgins who are ready for the bridegroom with oil in their lamps.

label: Disciples' weakness and denial
why: This phrase captures the core of the theme as seen in Peter's denial of Jesus three times, as predicted and described in Matthew 26:34, 69-75, Luke 22:34, 54-62, and John 21:15-19.

label: Anointing with perfume
why: Mark 14:3-9 and John 19:19-22 both highlight the anointing with ointment as a preparatory act, either for burial or for proclamation.

label: Burial and tomb security
why: Matthew 27:62-66 and John 19:42 describe the tomb being made secure, with guards placed and a stone rolled in front, using forms of ἀσφαλισθὲν and τάφος.

label: Beginning of Jesus' ministry
why: Mark 1:1-13 and Luke 1:1-4 frame the start of Jesus' public ministry, and this phrase captures the theme as the text itself would express it.

label: Jesus' teaching and authority
why: Passages like Mark 1:21-27 and Luke 4:16-21 highlight Jesus' teaching and the authority with which He speaks, while ἐπιτιμῶν (to rebuke/command) and διδαχή (teaching) are central to the theme.

label: Divine rescue of Peter
why: Acts 12:5-11 and Acts 16:25-34 both describe miraculous escapes from prison, using the words ἅλυσις (deliverance) and φυλακή (prison).

label: Calling of Barnabas and Saul
why: Acts 13:2-3 and 13:9 show the calling (προσκαλῶ) and revelation (ἐμφανίζω) of Saul/Paul for mission work.

label: Worship and modesty
why: 1 Corinthians 11:3-16 puts it this way, discussing the practice of covering the head during prayer and prophecy as an expression of order and modesty in worship.

label: Instructions regarding Timothy
why: The passages in 1 Timothy and others use παραγγελία (instruction) and Τιμόθεος (Timothy) to frame the theme of Paul's teachings and orders directed to Timothy.

label: Shared Suffering and Hope
why: This phrase captures the central dynamic of the passages, where encouragement (παρακαλέω, παράκλησις) is given and received in the context of suffering (θλῖψις), as seen in 2 Corinthians 1:3-7 and 7:4-7, and 1 Thessalonians 3:6-8.

label: Paul's sorrow and love for the Corinthians
why: 2 Corinthians 2:4 and 7:2-3, along with Galatians 4:19, express Paul's personal sorrow and love for the Corinthians and other communities, using forms of ἀγάπη (love) and λύπη (sorrow).

label: Jethro's visit and praise
why: Exodus 18:1-12 describes Jethro's arrival with Moses' family and his praise of God, making 'Jethro's coming' the central phrase capturing the theme.

label: Moses' intercession and request for God's presence
why: Exodus 33:12-16 and 1 Chronicles 16:23-33 emphasize God's presence and glory as central to His relationship with His people.

label: Nazirite vow and consecration
why: Numbers 6:2-21 and Judges 13:4-5, 7 describe the Nazirite's consecration to the Lord through vows and ritual purity.

label: Negative Report and Fear
why: Ezra 4:11-15, 19-20 puts it this way, describing the adversaries' claims about rebuilding Jerusalem as an act of rebellion and a threat to stability.

label: Water Crisis and Rebellion
why: The passages highlight water scarcity (mayim) and the resulting distress (tzarah) that leads to rebellion or crisis, as seen in Numbers 20 and Jeremiah 14.

label: Songs and memory
why: 2 Samuel 1:17-27 combines a song (שִׁיר) with remembrance (זָכַר) of Saul and Jonathan, while Numbers 21:16-18 reflects on journey and provision through song and memory of the well.

label: Moses' final instructions and death
why: Deuteronomy 32:44-52 records Moses' final speech and instructions to Israel before his death, and 'דָבַר' (to speak) is a key term in this context.

label: Legal protection and justice
why: The passages highlight the dual role of judgment and deliverance, especially in the context of leadership and justice, as seen in David's rule and the administration of refuge cities.

label: Cities of refuge
why: Joshua 21:13, 21, 27, 32, 38 refer to the cities of refuge, using מִקְלָט to describe their purpose.

label: Building an altar as a symbol
why: Joshua 22:10-12 describes the building of an altar on the east side of the Jordan, which is a border, causing concern among the tribes.

label: kindness and protection in leadership
why: The passages highlight leadership (office) and acts of kindness (garment, washing, protection), especially in the context of noble or royal behavior, as seen in Boaz, Solomon, and Jesus.

label: restoration of property and inheritance
why: The passages emphasize the concepts of redeeming property (גְּאֻלָּה) and securing one's inheritance (נַחֲלָה), especially in the context of land, family, and legacy.

label: divine calling and recognition
why: The passages emphasize being called by God (קָרָא) in moments of recognition or revelation (e.g., Samuel hearing 'Eli, Eli,' or Paul hearing a voice on the road to Damascus).

label: Returning sacred objects with tribute
why: John 14:16-17, 15:26, and 16:13 use this exact phrase to describe the Holy Spirit's role in guiding and testifying, central to the theme of returning sacred objects with tribute as both acts of truth and divine guidance.

label: Refuge and gathering of followers
why: The passages show David and others in roles of both leadership and subordination, especially in times of refuge and gathering followers.

label: Mediation and prevention of violence
why: Abigail acts to prevent violence by bringing a gift to David (1 Sam 25:13-31), and the passages in Galatians and 1 Timothy emphasize gentle correction and care for others' well-being.

label: submission and fear
why: These passages highlight the act of fearing authority (Solomon) and submitting to it by sending or yielding, as seen in Adonijah and Hiram.

label: divine judgment and removal
why: 1 Kings 2:26-27 and Zephaniah 1:17-18 use forms of פָּקַד (to reckon/punish) and דָּמָה (to cease) to describe divine judgment and removal.

label: healing through obedience
why: 2 Kings 5:1-14 describes Naaman's healing from leprosy, and 'cleansed from leprosy' captures the central motif of healing through obedience in the text.

label: refusal of material reward
gloss: nor will I go to you
why: Luke 7:7 records the centurion saying this, expressing his faith and refusal to require Jesus to come under his roof for healing.

label: Espionage and divine revelation
why: The phrase captures the motif of divine revelation through unusual or symbolic states (as in Isaiah 20:2-4) and the sending of messengers or spies (as in 2 Kings 6:8-13), while 'descended' reflects divine insight or presence.

label: Revelation and Consequence
why: The phrase encapsulates the idea of revelation and consequence, as seen in passages where divine truth emerges (Isaiah 39) or where outcomes unfold (2 Kings 7).

label: Anointing of a New King
why: The theme is centered on anointing, as seen in 2 Kings 9:1-10 where Jehu is anointed with oil as the new king.

label: Rise to power and transfer of authority
why: Esther 8:8-13 and 10:2-3 emphasize the king's sealing of decrees and the transfer of his signet ring, symbolizing the transfer of authority.

label: Description of divine creatures
why: Ezekiel 10:4-5, 8-11, 14-15, 16-17, 18-19, 20-22 describe the divine creatures (חַיּ֣וֹת) associated with the evening (עֵ֑רֶב) vision, emphasizing their form, wings, and connection to the glory of the Lord.

label: Rebuke and atonement
why: Luke 13:1-5 and other passages use this imperative form of μετανοῶ to warn of the need to turn from error and avoid destruction.

label: Supplication for mercy and deliverance
why: Psalms 79:8-9 and Lamentations 3:55-58 use this phrase to express the act of crying out to God for mercy and deliverance.

label: Affirmation of covenant and praise
why: Psalms 79:13 and 92:2-5, along with Isaiah 25:1, emphasize God's faithfulness and praise, often paired with the divine name.

label: Petition for Divine Intervention
gloss: call to the Lord for salvation
why: Psalms 80, 86, 88, and 90 repeatedly use forms of קָרָא (call) and יְשׁוּעָה (salvation) to express petition for divine intervention.

label: God's promise of blessing if Israel obeys
why: The passages emphasize obedience (do) and love for God and neighbor, especially in Mark 12:28-34 and Psalms 81:14-17.

label: God's judgment on false gods
why: Psalms 82, 96, and 97 emphasize God's judgment of false gods (elilim), while שָׁפַט (shofet) is the root verb used for this judgment.

label: Blessedness of dwelling with God
why: 2 Corinthians 5:1-5 speaks of a heavenly dwelling (σκῆνος) and being at home in the body or absent from the body, with the hope of being with the Lord, while other passages emphasize being with God (σὺν θεῷ) and heavenly dwelling.

label: God as protector and provider
why: This phrase captures the recurring contrast between God as light and the wicked as darkness, as seen in Psalms 97:10-12 and Ephesians 5:8-13, where God is depicted as the source of guidance, protection, and deliverance.

label: Faithful use of resources
why: Matthew 25:14-30 uses this phrase to describe the master entrusting resources to his servants, central to the theme of faithful use of resources.

label: Judgment and separation of people
why: Matthew 25:31-46 describes people being separated like sheep and goats, using this verb to express the act of judgment and division.

label: Guards' deception
why: Matthew 28:11-15 shows the guards being paid to announce a false account, making 'money announce' a concise phrase capturing the essence of the guards' deception.

label: Calling of the first disciples
why: Mark 1:17 and Luke 5:10 use this exact phrase to describe the new calling of the disciples.

label: God's wrath against ungodliness
why: Romans 1:18-25 explicitly speaks of 'God's wrath' being revealed against ungodliness and unrighteousness.

label: Variety of roles in the church
why: Ephesians 4:7-12 and 1 Corinthians 12:28-30 emphasize the diversity of spiritual gifts and roles in the church, using terms like χρῖσμα and διδασκαλος to describe them.

label: Collection for the saints
why: 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 and 2 Corinthians 8-9 use this phrase to describe the purpose of the collection.

label: Jethro's advice on leadership
why: Exodus 18:21-22 and 2 Chronicles 19:5-7 emphasize appointing judges (שׁוֹפְטִים) to oversee the people (הָעָם), central to Jethro's leadership model.

label: Protection of Women and Daughters
why: The passages highlight acts of protection and proper conduct, especially in 2 Chronicles 29 where Hezekiah offers sacrifices and restores worship, and in Exodus 21 and 1 Peter 3 where responsibilities toward women are emphasized.

label: Inclusivity in Passover
