label: God's Judgment and Mercy
why: The passages highlight God's judgment (wrath) and His forgiveness (mercy), as seen in Numbers 14, Psalms 106, and Matthew 13.

label: Divine validation of leadership
why: Numbers 17:17-25 describes the divine validation of Aaron's leadership through the sprouting rod, which serves as a testimony among the tribes.

label: Accessibility of the law
why: Deuteronomy 30:11-14 emphasizes that the law is near, in one's mouth and heart, using words like תּוֹרָה and פָּה.

label: Moses' farewell and succession
why: Deuteronomy 31 and Jeremiah 32-33 use these terms to frame the themes of exile and restoration central to Moses' farewell and succession.

label: The law as a witness
why: Deuteronomy 31:26 refers to the law placed near the ark as a witness.

label: vows and their tragic consequences
why: The phrase encapsulates the tragic fulfillment of vows, as seen in Judges 11:30-40 where Jephthah vows and then brings the consequence upon his daughter.

label: betrayal and deception by a woman
why: Judges 16:4-19 centers on Delilah's deception of Samson, using the verb תָּלַל ('to deceive') to describe her actions.

label: divine judgment on a family
why: 1 Samuel 2:22-36 directly refers to Eli's household as the subject of divine judgment.

label: Eli's Judgment
why: 1 Samuel 3:11-14 centers on Eli's judgment for his and his sons' iniquity, and the theme is echoed in John's witness (John 1:6-15, 3:22-30) as a preparatory judgment for the coming light.

label: capture of sacred symbols
why: 1 Samuel 4:11 describes the ark being captured and the Israelites fleeing, with the ark's fall marking a pivotal moment in the narrative.

label: Divine confirmation of return
gloss: ark of the house of God
why: The ark is repeatedly associated with the divine presence and the house of God in these passages, especially in its journey and eventual dwelling among the people.

label: Rivalry and persecution between kings
why: The passages emphasize conflict between rulers and their forces, using words like לָחַם (to fight) and חַ֫יִל (strength, soldiers), as seen in 1 Samuel 19 and Jeremiah 37.

label: Loyalty and covenant in friendship
why: The passages in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel contrast Jonathan's loyalty with Ahithophel's betrayal, using the words for 'counsel' (עֵצָה) and the context of treachery (as in Absalom's court).

label: Deception for necessity and survival
why: This phrase captures the tension between restraint (silence) and speech (lying or strategic disclosure), as seen in David's actions in 1 Samuel 21 and 27, and Jonah's reluctant confession in Jonah 1.

label: Betrayal and deceptive diplomacy
why: The passages emphasize scattering (פּוּץ and זָרָה) as a result of betrayal and deceptive actions, especially in 1 Chronicles and Ezekiel.

label: plague and intercession
why: 2 Samuel 24:16-17 and 1 Chronicles 21:14-15 refer to the plague as being sent by a divine messenger, emphasizing the role of the messenger in delivering the punishment and the intercession that halts it.

label: territorial organization
why: The passages emphasize territorial divisions (land) and familial or tribal organization (families), as seen in 1 Kings 4 and the references to family (מִשְׁפָּחָה) and land (אֶרֶץ).

label: Famine and moral collapse
why: 2 Kings 6:24-30 describes both famine (צָרָה) and moral collapse (שִׁחַת) through cannibalism and despair.

label: Selection and preparation of a queen
why: Esther 2:1-17 uses these terms to describe the setting (palace, house) and the selection process (maiden) for the new queen.

label: Mourning and repentance in crisis
why: Esther 4:1-3 uses this phrase to describe the outward signs of mourning and repentance in crisis.

label: Longing for respite and afterlife hope
why: This phrase captures the longing for respite and hope in the afterlife, as seen in passages like Job 14 and 2 Corinthians 5, which express waiting or hoping until death.

label: Invitation to observe creation
why: Psalms 96:11-12 and 98:7-8 use these words to describe the natural world rejoicing and singing in response to God's presence.

label: Call for divine justice
why: Psalms 79:10-12 and Jeremiah 10:25 use this phrase to describe the call for divine retribution and justice for the spilled blood of the faithful.

label: God's peace and salvation
why: Psalms 85:8-13 explicitly connects שָׁלוֹם (peace) and יֵשַׁע (salvation) as God's gifts to His people, and these terms are central to the theme across the passages.

label: Praise of beauty
why: Ezekiel 19:10-14 uses the vine as a metaphor for Israel's former glory, and the language of beauty and fruitfulness in Song of Songs aligns with this imagery.

label: Intimate love and longing
why: Song of Songs 8:7 speaks of love that is 'great' (רַב), and the theme of deep, intimate love is central to the text.

label: Divine judgment on Jerusalem and Judah
why: Isaiah 3 and Zephaniah 2 depict the downfall and desolation of Jerusalem and Judah, with שְׁמָמָה (devastation) as a central term, and Zion as the symbolic name for Jerusalem.

label: Famine of the Word
why: Amos 8:11-12 speaks of a famine of the word of the Lord (דְּבַר יְהוָה), which is the core of the theme.

label: Judas' remorse and death
why: Matthew 27:3-5 uses ἀργυρίον (money) and αἷμα (blood) to frame Judas' remorse and suicide, central to the theme.

label: Mocking of Jesus
gloss: to mock, to put on, clothing
why: Mark 15:16-20 and Matthew 27:27-31 describe the mocking of Jesus through dressing him in a robe, using these words.

label: Disciples' mission
why: Matthew 28:19 puts it this way, encapsulating the disciples' mission as given by Jesus.

label: Worship of the risen Christ
why: Matthew 28:9,17 and Mark 16:9-14 use forms of προσκυνῶ (to worship) and describe worship directed to the risen Jesus.

label: Healing and forgiveness
gloss: to raise up and to release
why: This phrase captures the central actions in the passages where Jesus raises up (heals) the paralytic and releases (forgives) his sins, as seen in Mark 2:3-12 and Luke 5:20-24.

label: Eating with sinners
why: This phrase captures the central action in passages like Mark 2:16-17 and Luke 5:27-32, where Jesus is criticized for dining with tax collectors and sinners.

label: Sabbath and human need
gloss: It is permitted on the Sabbath
why: Mark 2:23-27 and Luke 6:1-5 use this phrase to frame Jesus' defense of his disciples' Sabbath actions, emphasizing permissibility in service of human need.

label: Faith and prayer of the church
why: The passages emphasize the church's intercessory prayer (προσευχή) and standing by (παραστημι) in faith, especially for Peter and Paul.

label: Herod's downfall
why: Acts 12:18-23 shows Herod's downfall as he becomes arrogant and is judged by God.

label: Parting of Paul and Barnabas
why: Acts 15:39 describes Paul and Barnabas parting ways, with Paul refusing to take Mark along again.

label: The mission to Jews and Gentiles
gloss: light to the Gentiles and the people
why: This phrase captures the mission to both Jews and Gentiles, as seen in passages like Acts 26 and Titus 2, where the gospel is presented as bringing light and salvation to all peoples.

label: The importance of each member
why: The phrase 'every member' captures the emphasis on the value and role of each part of the body in 1 Corinthians 12:21-24, where all parts are essential.

label: Encouragement to pursue greater gifts
why: 1 Corinthians 12:31 puts it this way, urging believers to pursue greater spiritual gifts.

label: Authentic Ministry and Integrity
why: The passages emphasize the importance of genuine knowledge of God and Christ, which undergirds authentic ministry and integrity.

label: Moses' request to see God's glory
why: Exodus 33:18-23 records Moses' request to see God's glory, using the phrase in its most direct form.

label: Preparation for the Tabernacle
why: Exodus 35:1-19 and 1 Chronicles 15:1-13 both emphasize the preparation and gathering for the construction or relocation of the Tabernacle.

label: Defective priests and service
why: Leviticus 21:16-23 discusses priests with blemishes (מוּם) who are excluded from altar service, forming the core of this theme.

label: Moses' marriage criticized
why: Numbers 12:2 refers to the criticism of Moses' authority and speech, which is tied to his marriage.

label: Scouting the Promised Land
why: Numbers 13:1-26 describes the sending of spies to explore Canaan, using the verb תּוּר ('to spy') and referring to the land (אֶרֶץ) of Canaan (כְּנַעַן).

label: Moses' plea for justice
why: This phrase captures the essence of Moses' plea for justice, as seen in Numbers 16:22 where he asks for action to cease until a resolution is reached, and in Ezra 4:21-24 where work is halted until a royal decree is issued.

label: Perpetual law
why: The phrase encapsulates the concept of a perpetual law, as seen in Numbers 19 where the purification process is established as an eternal statute for Israel.

label: Divine Judgment on Moses and Aaron
why: Jonah 1:5-7 describes Jonah sleeping while the sailors are in distress, and the phrase 'he slept in his mouth' captures the inaction and silence of Jonah, paralleling Moses' and Aaron's failure to speak or act in faith.

label: Journey through the wilderness
why: The passages in Numbers and Ezra describe the journey through the wilderness, and the word מִדְבָּר appears prominently in these texts as the setting for the journey.

label: Balak's attempt to curse Israel through Balaam
why: Numbers 22:5-15 describes Balak sending messengers to Balaam to curse Israel.

label: Joshua's farewell address
why: Joshua's farewell address emphasizes God's promise to give the land and the need to remain faithful to it.

label: linguistic conflict and discrimination
why: Judges 12:5-6 uses this word to show how linguistic differences led to conflict and discrimination between Ephraimites and Gileadites.

label: legal customs of redemption
why: The passages in Ruth and 2 Chronicles use these terms to describe the legal and covenantal acts of redemption and loyalty.

label: marriage for family legacy
why: Ruth 4:5-10 and 1 Samuel 25:32-42 both involve taking a woman as wife to fulfill a redemptive or restorative role in the family line.

label: Hannah's longing for a child
gloss: a woman whose womb is shut
why: 1 Samuel 1 describes Hannah as a woman whose womb is closed, and this phrase captures the central longing and condition in the narrative.

label: divine reversal of human status
why: This phrase captures the central idea of divine reversal of human status, as seen in passages like 1 Samuel 2 and Psalms 113, where God exalts the humble and abases the proud.

label: Eli's Death
why: 1 Samuel 4:18 describes Eli falling backward upon hearing of the ark's capture and his sons' deaths, marking the moment of his demise.

label: Loyalty and protection in friendship
why: The passages center on the loyalty between Jonathan and David, particularly in 1 Samuel 19:2-5 where Jonathan protects David from Saul.

label: Escape and deception for survival
why: 1 Samuel 19:11-14 describes David escaping (מָלַט) from Saul through Michal's deception (מִכְרָא is a root meaning 'deceit'), making it central to the theme.

label: Divine intervention in pursuit
why: 1 Samuel 19:20-21 describes how the messengers sent by Saul were overcome and began to prophesy, capturing the divine intervention in pursuit theme.

label: Anger and accusation in leadership
why: 1 Samuel 20 and 2 Samuel 20 show leaders like Saul and Joab expressing אַף (anger) and leveling accusations (דִּבְרֵי חֵטְא) against those they see as disloyal.

label: Paranoia and accusation in leadership
why: 1 Samuel 22:6-8 shows Saul accusing and standing against David, capturing the theme of paranoia and accusation in leadership.

label: Divine guidance in military decisions
gloss: to go by the word of God
why: The passages show David and Joab acting in accordance with divine instruction before engaging in battle, as seen in 1 Samuel 23:2 and 1 Chronicles 19:13.

label: Mercy and restraint in power
why: 1 Samuel 24:4-12 describes David cutting the edge of Saul's robe instead of killing him, symbolizing restraint and mercy.

label: marriage and foundation
why: 1 Kings 3:1-4 describes Solomon building a house (temple) for the LORD, linking the theme of foundation with the act of building, central to the narrative.

label: Divine intervention in food shortages
why: This phrase captures the miraculous multiplication of food in 2 Kings 4:42-44, where Elisha pours out (יָצַק) food that is sufficient (הִיָּה לַכֹּל) for many, and the Gerasene demoniac (Γερασηνης) proclaims salvation to all (παντι).

label: Divine provision and protection
why: This phrase, used in the context of divine action, appears in passages where God demonstrates provision and protection, such as in 2 Kings 6 and Acts 19.

label: Famine and Prophecy
why: The passages emphasize prophecy (דָבָר) and its fulfillment in a specific time (עֵת), as seen in Elisha's prediction and its timing in 2 Kings 7.

label: Famine and Displacement
why: The passages emphasize a seven-year period of displacement (2 Kings 8:1-3) and use terms like שֶׁבַע (seven) and גּוּר (to sojourn).

label: Restoration of Property
why: 2 Kings 8:4-6 refers to the woman's restoration of her land and house, making these terms central to the theme.

label: Death of Joram and Ahaziah
why: 2 Kings 9:14-27 describes the death of both Joram and Ahaziah, central to the theme.

label: Fate of Jezebel
why: 2 Kings 9:30-36 describes the fulfillment of prophecy through Jezebel's violent death, making her death central to the theme.

label: Jehu's partial righteousness
why: 2 Kings 10:29-31 notes Jehu's partial righteousness by saying he did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam.

label: Royal display and authority
why: Esther 1 and Ecclesiastes 8 emphasize the king's rule and authority, using the words מֶ֫לֶךְ and מָלַךְ to describe his sovereign power.

label: Genocidal plot and religious persecution
why: Esther 3:6-8 describes Haman's formulation of a plan to destroy all the Jews, and the language of 'plans' or 'thoughts' (machshavot) is central to the theme of genocidal intent.

label: Authorizing and spreading a destructive decree
why: Esther 3:12-13 describes Haman writing a decree (כָּתַב) for the destruction (אָבַד) of the Jews, which is then spread to all provinces.

label: Humiliation and despair of an antagonist
why: Esther 8:1-2, 7 mentions the giving of Haman's house to Esther, central to the theme of his downfall and the antagonist's humiliation.

label: Plea for reversal of a decree
why: Esther 8:3-6 shows Esther pleading with the king to reverse Haman's decree, using the phrase 'before the king' and the verb 'turn' in the context of seeking his favor and action.

label: Wisdom and authority of a speaker
why: Job 36 and Psalms 1 emphasize the contrast between the speech of the righteous and the wicked, using מִלָּה (speech), כִּי (for), and צַדִּיק (righteous) to frame the theme.

label: Majesty of God's Name
gloss: the name of the LORD is great
why: Psalms 8:1-2, 10 declares the greatness of God's name over all the earth, using שֵׁם, יְהוָה, and אַדִּיר.

label: sacred gesture of blessing
why: Psalms 134:2 uses this phrase to describe the gesture of blessing toward the holy place.

label: oath to remember Jerusalem
gloss: Jerusalem shall not be forgotten from our memory
why: Psalms 137:5-6 express the vow not to forget Jerusalem, using forms of 'לֹא' (not), 'יְרוּשָׁלִַם' (Jerusalem), and the idea of memory.

label: Foreign invasion and desecration
why: Psalms 79:1-4 and Micah 4:9-10 describe foreign forces coming around Jerusalem to invade and desecrate it.

label: Historical Memory and Divine Provision
why: Psalms 89:50-53 explicitly calls on God to remember His covenant with His people, central to the theme of historical memory and divine provision.

label: Call to divine action
why: This phrase encapsulates the divine action of God in upholding justice and righteousness, as seen in Psalms 82:8 and Isaiah 26:8-10, 16-18.

label: God's Enemies Plot Against Israel
why: Psalms 83:3-9 describes nations plotting (ya'ats) against Israel, using im (with) and describing their evil intent.

label: Judgment and Destruction of the Wicked
why: Psalms 83:10-16 and 86:8-9 use this phrase to describe God's presence and judgment, central to the theme of divine judgment and destruction of the wicked.

label: Symbolic natural imagery
why: Song of Songs 4:1-15 uses garden imagery to describe the beloved's beauty and allure, central to the theme of symbolic natural imagery.

label: Intimacy and union
why: Song of Songs 4:12-15 uses this imagery to describe a sealed garden and a flowing spring, symbolizing intimacy and union.

label: Desire and longing
why: John 4:24 uses this exact phrase to describe the nature of true worship, central to the theme of desire and longing expressed through spiritual connection.

label: love and longing
why: The motif of 'open hand' appears in passages involving longing and love, such as Song of Songs 5:2-6, and is also used metaphorically in passages about compassion and repentance, like Luke 15:4-7.

label: Desire and mutual affection
why: John 4:10-14 uses this phrase to describe the spiritual sustenance Jesus offers, central to the theme of desire and mutual affection.

label: God's patient waiting
why: Mark 13 emphasizes God's waiting for the elect to be delivered, using forms of παραδώσωμι and ἐκλεκτός to frame divine patience and selection.

label: New creation and renewal
why: Isaiah 65:17 speaks of a new creation (בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה), and Ephesians 1:10 speaks of the renewal of all things in Christ.

label: Watchman and responsibility
why: Ezekiel 33:1-20 emphasizes the watchman's duty to rise and warn of judgment, using forms of 'rise' (קוּם) and 'warn' (זָהַר).

label: Jesus' withdrawal and mission
why: Mark 1:35-39 and 8:11-13 show Jesus going out (ἐξέρχομαι) and preaching (κηρύσσω), central to his withdrawal and mission.

label: Calling a tax collector
why: Jesus calls Levi to 'follow him' (Mark 2:14), and this phrase is central to the theme of being called and responding to Jesus.

label: Fasting and new teachings
why: Mark 2:18-22 and Mark 9:2-8 highlight Jesus' new teachings and divine identity, using καινὰς (new) and γνῶσις (knowledge) to signify the novelty and depth of his message.

label: Mission to Cyprus and conflict with a false prophet
why: Acts 13:8-10 and 23:23-35 describe figures who oppose and hinder Paul's mission, using forms of ἀντί (against) and παρεμποδίζω (to hinder).

label: Miraculous healing and idolatry
why: Acts 24:5 and 9 show the accusation against Paul involving divine implications, while Acts 14 shows the crowd mistaking him for a god.

label: The Jerusalem Council
why: Acts 15:6-21 describes the gathering of apostles and elders to resolve the issue of Gentile inclusion, using this structure to name the council.

label: The Letter to Antioch
why: Acts 15:22-29 describes the sending of a letter by the apostles and elders to Antioch, and the language of selection (ἐκλεγω) and sending (ἀποστολος) is central to the theme.

label: The Conversion of Lydia
why: This phrase captures the act of invoking or appealing to a name, central to Lydia's conversion and the legal proceedings involving Paul and Festus.

label: The Demon-Possessed Slave Girl
why: Acts 16:16 refers to the girl 'having a spirit of divination,' which is πνεῦμα προφητεύων in the original Greek, central to the theme.

label: The resurrection of the dead
why: The phrase captures the core idea of resurrection, as seen in passages like Acts 26 where Paul discusses the resurrection of the dead as a central tenet of faith.

label: Paul's miraculous survival on Melita
why: Acts 28 describes Paul being saved (διασῴζω) on the island (γῆ), and the theme centers on his miraculous deliverance there.

label: Love is superior to spiritual gifts
why: 1 Corinthians 13:1-3 and James 2:14-26 both emphasize that spiritual gifts and faith are ineffective χωρὶς ἀγάπην.

label: Characteristics of love
why: 1 Corinthians 13 and Titus 3 both highlight love's expression through good works, using forms of προστίθημι and καλὰ ἔργα.

label: Order and maturity in worship
why: 1 Corinthians 14 emphasizes order (κατὰ τάξιν) and spiritual maturity (πνεῦμα), aligning with the theme of order and maturity in worship.

label: The necessity of resurrection for believers
why: 1 Corinthians 15 and 1 Thessalonians 4 both use forms of ἀνάστασις and νεκρός to frame the central hope and necessity of resurrection for believers.

label: God's refusal to accompany Israel
gloss: I will not go up in their midst
why: Exodus 33:3-5 expresses God's refusal to accompany Israel in their journey because of their sinfulness.

label: Moses' Radiance
why: Exodus 34:29-35 describes Moses' face shining (קָרַן) and his skin (עוֹר) glowing after speaking with God, and the term is central to the theme.

label: Joshua and Caleb's Loyalty
gloss: I will spy for the LORD
why: Numbers 14:6-9 shows Caleb's declaration of loyalty to the LORD by affirming the land and urging trust in Him, using these key words.

label: Public demonstration of divine will
why: Numbers 16:31-35 describes the earth swallowing the rebels, illustrating divine judgment through a public, physical demonstration.

label: Purification ritual for contact with death
why: Numbers 19:2-22 describes the purification ritual using a red heifer as central to the process of cleansing from contact with death.

label: Ritual impurity from death
why: Numbers 19:11-16 describes how a person becomes ritually unclean by touching a dead body, using the words נָגַע ('touch') and מוֹת ('death').

label: Diplomatic Attempt with Edom
gloss: send envoys to the king of Edom
why: Numbers 20:14-21 describes Moses sending envoys to the king of Edom to request passage, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Divine intervention through Balaam's donkey
gloss: angel of God on Balaam's way
why: Numbers 22:22-31 describes the messenger of the LORD blocking Balaam's journey, revealed through the donkey's miraculous awareness.

label: Balaam's eventual compliance under divine guidance
gloss: the word that the Lord puts in the mouth
why: Numbers 22:35, 38 show Balaam speaking only what God commands him to speak.

label: Moses' Blessing of the Tribes
why: Deuteronomy 33:1-29 contains Moses' blessings to each of the tribes of Israel, using the word בְּרָכָה ('blessing') and referring to the twelve tribes (שִׁבְטִים).

label: Moses' final view of the Promised Land
why: Deuteronomy 34:1-4 describes Moses seeing the land from the mountain, using these exact words.

label: Moses' death and burial
why: Deuteronomy 34:5-6 describes Moses' death and burial in Moab, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Moses' physical condition at death
gloss: his eyes and strength did not fail
why: Deuteronomy 34:7 puts it this way, describing Moses' physical condition at death.

label: Mourning for Moses
why: Deuteronomy 34:8 describes the Israelites mourning Moses, and the phrase 'בְּכִי אַהֲרֹן' is used in similar contexts for mourning a leader.

label: Legal protection and justice
why: Joshua 20:3, 6 refer to cities of refuge for the unintentional murderer, using מִקְלַט and נֶ֫פֶשׁ.

label: Legal protection and justice
why: Joshua 20:3-6 refers to these cities as places of refuge for those who have committed unintentional homicide.

label: Legal protection and justice
why: Joshua 20:9 refers to these cities as places of refuge for those seeking legal protection.

label: Accusation of rebellion
why: Joshua 22:17-18 puts the accusation of rebellion (מָרַד) against the congregation (עֵדָה) at the heart of the conflict over the altar.

label: Defense of the altar
why: Joshua 22:20-29 explains the altar was built as a witness (עֵד) to their commitment, not for sacrifice (זֶבַח), making 'witness altar' the most fitting phrase.

label: communal validation of transactions
why: Ruth 4:2,9,11 put it this way to describe the communal validation of transactions through witnesses, the people, and elders.

label: divine blessing and ancestral lineage
why: Ruth 4:11-17 emphasizes the restoration of lineage and divine blessing through the naming and continuation of the household (be'it) of the ancestor (av), particularly through the naming (shem) of Obed, the son of Ruth and Boaz.

label: honesty and obedience in prophecy
gloss: all the word that was told
why: 1 Samuel 3:15-18 puts it this way, describing Samuel's full disclosure of the message he received from the LORD.

label: A Tragic Birth
why: 1 Samuel 4:20-22 describes the tragic birth and the loss of divine glory, where the word 'גָּלָה' (to reveal/remove) and 'כָּבוֹד' (glory) are central.

label: Plague in Ashdod
why: The phrase captures the central event described in 1 Samuel 5:6-7, where a plague (חֶבֶל) strikes the city of Ashdod (אַשְׁדּוֹד).

label: Moving the Ark to Gath
why: 1 Samuel 5:8-9 uses this phrase to describe the action of moving or turning the Ark to Gath.

label: Plague Spreads to Ekron
why: 1 Samuel 5:10-11 describes the ongoing plague in Ekron after the Ark's arrival, using terms like מַחֲלָה (plague) and describing its spreading effects.

label: Plague and divine distress
why: 1 Samuel 5:12 describes the city being overwhelmed by the plague, using the word 'chevel' to denote the affliction.

label: Seeking guidance on sacred objects
why: 1 Samuel 6:2-5 focuses on the Philistines seeking guidance on how to return the ark to Israel, making 'return the ark' the central phrase.

label: Fear and anxiety in danger
why: 1 Samuel 20:3 puts David's anxious actions at the center, describing what he did in fear of Saul.

label: Secret communication and strategy
why: 1 Samuel 20 describes how Jonathan uses an arrow as a signal to communicate secretly with David, making 'arrow to David' a central motif of the passage.

label: Fear and uncertainty in leadership
why: 1 Samuel 23:3 captures the sentiment of fear (פַּחַד) and vulnerability/uncertainty (עֶבְרָה) in leadership.

label: Moral restraint and reverence for authority
why: 1 Samuel 24:5-6 shows David refusing to harm Saul, emphasizing that he will not raise his hand against the Lord’s anointed, reflecting moral restraint and reverence for divine authority.

label: loyalty and valor in service
why: 2 Samuel 23:8-39 refers to David’s loyal and courageous warriors as gibborim, and the theme centers on their valor and service.

label: divine judgment and human choice
why: 2 Samuel 24:11-14 shows David choosing between judgments, and the language of choice (בָּחַר) and iniquity (עָוֹן) is central to the theme.

label: altar and atonement
gloss: altar to offer a burnt offering
why: 2 Samuel 24:25 describes David building an altar and offering burnt offerings to atone and stop the plague.

label: aging and legacy
why: 1 Kings 1:2-4 uses this phrase to describe David's aging and the need for a new heir, framing the theme of aging and legacy in terms of physical decline and the loss of youthful beauty.

label: succession and rebellion
why: 1 Kings 1:5-10 centers on Adonijah's attempt to claim the throne, using his name and the theme of kingship (מַלְכּוּת).

label: population and prosperity
why: 1 Kings 4:20 describes the large and prosperous population, using terms that align with these words.

label: Leprosy and Survival
why: The theme is captured in the tension between the lepers' decision to 'dwell' (יָשַׁב) in the risk of 'coming' (בּוֹא) to the camp, facing 'death' (מָוֶת), as described in 2 Kings 7:3-5.

label: Jehu's purge of Ahab's house
why: 2 Kings 10:1-11, 17 refers to Jehu's killing of Ahab's seventy sons, central to the purge of Ahab's house.

label: Elimination of Baal worship
why: 2 Kings 10:18-27 describes Jehu's campaign to destroy Baal worship, including the killing of his priests and the elimination of his altars.

label: Foreign influence and opposition
why: Nehemiah 6:17-19 puts Tobiah and Judah in direct opposition, showing his influence and conflict with Judah.

label: Disobedience and consequences in royal court
why: Esther 1:8-12 and related passages focus on the queen in the royal court and the consequences of her disobedience.

label: Loyalty and guardianship in royal service
why: Esther 2:19-21 and 2:23 describe Mordecai's role in guarding the king's gate and protecting the palace, reflecting his loyalty and guardianship in royal service.

label: Protection and justice in the palace
why: Esther 2:21-23 refers to events occurring on the king's day, highlighting the palace setting and the urgency of justice and protection.

label: Rise of an antagonist and personal grievance
why: Esther 3:2-5 puts this phrase at the heart of Haman's grievance and the rising conflict.

label: Execution of a destructive decree
why: Esther 3:12 and 3:14 describe the decree (law) being given and enacted throughout the kingdom.

label: Communication and urgency in crisis
why: Esther 4:8 and 4:14 use these words to describe Mordecai’s urgent message to Esther about Haman’s plot.

label: Risk and danger in royal action
why: Esther 4:11 uses the word 'צַיִד' to describe the peril involved in approaching the king without being summoned.

label: Divine purpose and moral responsibility
phrase: כִּי לֹא לַבְּלִיָּה אַתְּ מָצָאתִיָּה בָּזְמַן הַזֶּה
translit: ki lo labliyah atem matsatiyah bazman haze
gloss: for you were not brought here for nothing at this time
why: Esther 4:14 puts it this way, emphasizing divine purpose and moral responsibility.

label: Preparation and communal prayer
why: Esther 4:15-17 refers to the call for fasting and prayer among all the Jews as part of the communal preparation.

label: Uninvited audience and royal favor
why: Esther 5:1-2 describes Esther appearing before the king uninvited, using the phrase 'stood before the king' to convey her unexpected audience with him.

label: Royal favor and promise of aid
why: Esther 5:3-6 shows the king offering to give (נָתַן) whatever request (בַּקָּשָׁה) Esther makes.

label: Strategic invitation and delay of action
why: Esther 5:4-8 shows Esther using a banquet to delay her request, making this phrase capture the strategic invitation and postponement of action.

label: Antagonism and escalation of conflict
why: The conflict between Mordecai and Haman is central to the escalation of antagonism in Esther 5:9-14 and throughout the book.

label: Recognition of past service and honor
why: Esther 6:3 puts it this way when the king asks what should be done to honor Mordecai for his past service.

label: Suggesting honor for the king
why: Esther 6:4-9 describes Haman suggesting a display of honor for the king, using forms of יְקָר and מֶ֫לֶךְ central to the theme.

label: Unexpected honor and reversal
why: Esther 6:11 describes Haman being forced to clothe the horse for Mordecai, symbolizing his unexpected reversal of honor.

label: Revelation and plea for salvation
why: Esther 7:3-4 connects the plight of the people (עַם) with a plea to the king (מֶלֶךְ) for their salvation.

label: Exposure and condemnation of an enemy
why: Esther 7:5-10 describes Haman being condemned and hanged on the tree, making this phrase central to the theme of exposure and condemnation of an enemy.

label: Royal anger and execution of justice
why: Esther 7:7-8, 10 describe the king's fury (חֵמָה) toward Haman and his subsequent execution, making this phrase central to the theme.

label: Futility of human wisdom
why: Job 12:12, 17-20 uses forms of 'sholal' (barefoot, futility) and 'halakhah' (to go, take a path) to describe the ineffectiveness of human wisdom and power in the face of divine will.

label: Hope in a future redeemer
why: Job 19:25-27 uses this phrase to express his vision of a future Redeemer, capturing the personal and prophetic nature of the theme.

label: Wisdom and its pursuit
why: Job 28:12-22 repeatedly asks where wisdom can be found, using מָקוֹם ('place') and חַכְמָה ('wisdom') to frame the theme of wisdom's elusive location and pursuit.

label: Instinct and natural behavior
why: Job 39:14-18 uses this phrase to emphasize that animals act instinctively, not by reason or human instruction.

label: nighttime worship
why: Psalms 134:1 refers to the house of the Lord at night, and 'house of testimony' is a common designation for the temple in the Hebrew Bible.

label: refusal to sing in a foreign land
gloss: we will not sing in a foreign land
why: Psalms 137:4 expresses this refusal directly in these words.

label: Threats to the Vine (Israel)
why: Psalms 80:13-14, 17 uses 'gefen' to symbolize Israel's vulnerability and destruction.

label: Advocacy for the vulnerable
why: Psalms 82:3-4 calls for defending the poor, using the word דַּל (dāl) in the context of their vulnerability.

label: Call to God for Action
why: Psalms 83:2, 14-16 show the psalmist calling out to God for action, using language of raising or lifting a plea to Him.

label: Recognition of God's Sovereignty
why: Psalms 83:17-19 calls for enemies to recognize the name of the LORD, signifying his sovereignty.

label: Longing for God's presence
why: Psalms 84:2-4 express a deep yearning for God's presence, using language of longing and sacred spaces.

label: Supremacy of God's house
why: Psalms 84:11 refers to the courts of God's house, emphasizing its supreme value.

label: Request for restoration
why: Psalms 85:5-7 uses this phrase to express the plea for God to restore His favor.

label: romantic pursuit and rejection
why: The theme is reflected in the pursuit (seeking) and the absence or failure to find, as in Song of Songs 5:6-7.

label: beauty and admiration
why: Song of Songs 5:10-16 uses these terms to describe the beloved's physical beauty and the admiration for him.

label: Lovers' separation and reunion
why: Song of Songs 6:1-3 expresses longing for the return of the beloved, emphasizing their absence.

label: Comparison to many others
why: Song of Songs 6:8-9 distinguishes the beloved as a queen among many others, using the language of comparison and uniqueness.

label: Mysterious transformation
why: Song of Songs 6:11-12 uses this phrase to describe a sudden, mysterious experience of transformation or elevation, possibly in a dream or vision.

label: Physical beauty of the beloved
why: Song of Songs 7:6-8 uses this phrase to highlight the beloved's physical beauty in comparison to others.

label: Preparation for a shared future
why: Song of Songs 7:12-14 implies a shared future through the act of giving, using 'נָתַן' and addressing 'ךְ' as part of a mutual journey with the beloved.

label: Cultural and familial roles
why: Song of Songs 8:8-10 uses these terms to reflect on familial and cultural roles, particularly in relation to care and protection.

label: Economic metaphor and ownership
why: Song of Songs 8:12 uses the vineyard and its fruit as a metaphor for care and yield in relationship.

label: God's power over nations
gloss: The LORD works with His hand, like clay
why: Jeremiah 18:4-6 uses this imagery to show God's power over Israel, forming and reshaping as a potter with clay.

label: remnant of Jacob's strength
why: Micah 5:6-7 refers to the remnant of Jacob as a central figure in the passage, describing its strength and flourishing.

label: spiritual connection and fruitfulness
gloss: to bear fruit in the vine
why: John 15:4-5 uses these words to describe the spiritual connection and fruitfulness that comes from remaining in Jesus, the true vine.

label: Divine guidance through visions
why: Acts 10 describes both Peter and Cornelius receiving divine guidance through visions (ὅραμα) and hearing a voice (φωνή) from heaven.

label: Cornelius as a model of faith and devotion
why: Acts 10:2 describes Cornelius as one who gave charity and feared God.

label: The proclamation of Jesus as Lord of all
why: Acts 10:36-43 proclaims Jesus as the one who is Lord over all people, both Jews and Gentiles.

label: Prophetic guidance and communal response
why: Acts 11:27-30 shows a prophet predicting famine (διὰ προφήτου) and the community responding (εἰς ἀποκρίσιν) by sending aid.

label: Preparation for Paul's appeal to Caesar
why: Acts 25:11-12 records Paul's declaration that he appeals to Caesar, and Festus confirms this as the course of action.

label: Paul's defense before Agrippa
why: Acts 26:1-29 records Paul's defense before King Agrippa, using the words ἀπολογέομαι and Ἀγρίππας prominently.

label: The reaction of the court
why: Acts 26:24-32 features King Agrippa as a central figure in the court's reaction to Paul's defense.

label: Paul's voyage to Italy
why: Acts 27:4, 27:12, and 27:27 describe Paul's voyage, his position on the ship, and his status as a prisoner.

label: Paul's warning of danger
why: Acts 27:9-10, 21-22, 25-26 put Paul's warning in terms of παραινῶν (urging) and πλοῖον (voyage/boat) as central to his message.

label: Divine intervention and reassurance
why: Acts 27:23-25 shows Paul's reassurance rooted in divine presence and promise, using forms of θεός, με, and παραστήσει.

label: Survival and landing on an island
why: Acts 27:44 describes how all were saved (διασῴζω) and brought to land (ἐπὶ αἰγιαλῷ), capturing the survival and landing on an island theme.

label: Healing and hospitality in Melita
why: Acts 28:9 describes Paul's healing actions (ἐπιτίθημι) taking place on the island (νῆσος), central to the theme.

label: Paul's journey to Rome
why: Acts 28:11-14 describes Paul's journey to Rome, and the verb ἐπιμένω (remain/keep on) and preposition εἰς (toward) are central to the narrative of his journey.

label: Paul's meeting with Jewish leaders in Rome
why: Acts 28:19 uses this phrase as Paul explains his situation to Jewish leaders in Rome, emphasizing his innocence and purpose.

label: Paul's proclamation of the gospel in Rome
why: Acts 28:23-31 shows Paul proclaiming the gospel in Rome, using περὶ (about) and λαλῶν (speaking), with θεός (God) as central to his message.

label: Love endures and outlasts
why: 1 Corinthians 13:8-13 emphasizes that love endures and outlasts all else, using the phrase 'agape' for love and 'menō' for remains.

label: Partial knowledge and growth
why: 1 Corinthians 13:9-12 discusses the idea of partial knowledge (μέρος γνῶσις) that will be replaced by full knowledge.

label: Spiritual gifts and their purpose
why: 1 Corinthians 14 repeatedly discusses spiritual gifts (πνεύματα) and their function within the context of the church (ἐκκλησίᾳ).

label: Clarity in communication
why: 1 Corinthians 14:13-17 and 27-28 emphasize the need for interpretation when someone speaks in tongues, making this phrase central to the theme of clarity in communication.

label: Edification of the church
why: 1 Corinthians 14:3-4, 12, 26, 31, 40 emphasize that all activities in the church should be done for the building up (οἰκοδομή) of the congregation (ἐκκλησία).

label: Role of women in worship
why: 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 addresses women in the context of the assembly, using these terms to frame the issue.

label: The resurrection of Christ
why: The verb ἐγείρω is central to the language of resurrection in the New Testament, including in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, where it is used to describe the resurrection of Jesus.

label: Christ as the firstfruits of resurrection
why: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 presents Christ as the firstfruits of those who have died.

label: The nature of the resurrection body
why: 1 Corinthians 15:44 and 1 Corinthians 15:46 contrast the natural body with the spiritual body, using these exact terms to describe the nature of the resurrection body.

label: Victory over death
why: 1 Corinthians 15:50-58 describes the triumph of believers over death, using νῖκος for 'victory' and θάνατος for 'death'.

label: Paul's travel plans
why: 1 Corinthians 16:5-9 uses these words to express Paul's conditional plans to stay in certain places depending on circumstances.

label: Exhortations to the community
why: 1 Corinthians 16:13-18 addresses the community collectively, using terms like πᾶς (all) and ἐν (in/among) to frame exhortations directed to the whole group.

label: God's Work in the Believers
why: This phrase from Philippians 2:13 captures the essence of God's active role in believers, aligning with the theme of God's work in the believers as seen in 2 Corinthians 1:21-22.

label: Hypocrisy and false claims
why: This term is used in the New Testament to describe those who claim to know God but deny Him through their actions, as seen in passages like Titus 1:16.

label: New creation and restoration
why: 2 Peter 3:13 refers to the new creation in Greek as 'καινὴ κτίσις'.

label: conflict with false leaders
why: 3 John 1:10 refers to the author welcoming missionaries, contrasting with Diotrephes' opposition.

label: Apocalyptic visions and seals
why: Revelation 6:1-17 repeatedly uses this structure to introduce each of the apocalyptic visions as the Lamb opens the seals.

label: Apocalyptic visions and divine silence
why: Revelation 8:1 uses imagery of silence in heaven, which echoes the Hebrew concept of Sheol as a place of silence and absence of divine presence.

label: Divine messengers and judgment
why: Revelation 8:2-6 refers to the seven angels who are given authority and trumpets to sound, central to the theme of divine messengers and judgment.
